Friendship jealousy is expected to be more prominent in some cultures than in others due to the differential importance placed on the maintenance of close, non-kin, non-romantic social bonds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=Corey L. |last2=Krems |first2=Jaimie Arona |last3=Kenrick |first3=Douglas T. |date=2021 |title=Fundamental Motives Illuminate a Broad Range of Individual and Cultural Variations in Thought and Behavior |journal=Current Directions in Psychological Science |language=en |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=242–250 |doi=10.1177/0963721421996690 |issn=0963-7214}}</ref> Relatedly, cultures in which friendships are highly valued, such as those marked by [[Individualistic culture|individualism]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Peiqi |last2=Oh |first2=Jeewon |last3=Leahy |first3=Katelin E. |last4=Chopik |first4=William J. |date=2021-01-18 |title=Friendship Importance Around the World: Links to Cultural Factors, Health, and Well-Being |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=11 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2020.570839 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=7848226 |pmid=33536962}}</ref> are likely to yield higher levels of friendship jealousy. In some cultures, however, avoiding overt expressions of conflict is essential in maintaining positive friendships,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=French |first1=Doran C. |last2=Pidada |first2=Sri |last3=Denoma |first3=Jill |last4=McDonald |first4=Kristina |last5=Lawton |first5=Allison |date=2005 |title=Reported Peer Conflicts of Children in the United States and Indonesia |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9507.2005.00311.x |journal=Social Development |language=en |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=458–472 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9507.2005.00311.x |issn=0961-205X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> so certain displays of friendship jealousy may be [[Social stigma|stigmatized]] and less likely to occur. In alignment with research on cross-cultural differences in the link between romantic jealousy and permissiveness toward [[extramarital sex]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Scelza |first1=Brooke A. |last2=Prall |first2=Sean P. |last3=Blumenfield |first3=Tami |last4=Crittenden |first4=Alyssa N. |last5=Gurven |first5=Michael |last6=Kline |first6=Michelle |last7=Koster |first7=Jeremy |last8=Kushnick |first8=Geoff |last9=Mattison |first9=Siobhán M. |last10=Pillsworth |first10=Elizabeth |last11=Shenk |first11=Mary K. |last12=Starkweather |first12=Kathrine |last13=Stieglitz |first13=Jonathan |last14=Sum |first14=Chun-Yi |last15=Yamaguchi |first15=Kyoko |date=2020 |title=Patterns of paternal investment predict cross-cultural variation in jealous response |journal=Nature Human Behaviour |language=en |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=20–26 |doi=10.1038/s41562-019-0654-y |issn=2397-3374 |pmc=8006540 |pmid=31332300}}</ref> it is also likely that sociocultural norms concerning friendship exclusivity might influence the experience of friendship jealousy.

=== Individual differences ===

==== Self-esteem ====
Having low [[self-esteem]] has been associated with increased [[vulnerability]] to friendship jealousy.<ref name=":2" /> This pattern can be explained by the [[Social comparison theory|upward social comparisons]] those with low self-esteem perform when assessing a rival; concluding that one's rival is more valuable than oneself will lead to increased replacement threat, and a resulting increase in friendship jealousy. At the same time, having an inflated self-esteem might also increase friendship jealousy vulnerability due to the instability and fragility which characterize unrealistically high levels of self-esteem.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Baumeister |first=R. F. |title=The handbook of social psychology |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=1998 |editor-last=Gilbert |editor-first=D. T. |edition=4th |location=New York, NY |pages=680–740 |chapter=The self |editor-last2=Fiske |editor-first2=S. T. |editor-last3=Lindzey |editor-first3=G.}}</ref> An individual with an inflated self-esteem is more likely to perceive [[Ambiguity|ambiguous]] [[Stimulus (psychology)|stimuli]] in ego-threatening ways.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heatherton |first1=Todd F. |last2=Vohs |first2=Kathleen D. |date=2000 |title=Interpersonal evaluations following threats to self: Role of self-esteem |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=78 |issue=4 |pages=725–736 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.78.4.725 |pmid=10794376 |issn=0022-3514}}</ref> For example, if a person with an inflated self-esteem witnesses their best friend engaging in conversation with a third-party, they might assume that their status in their best friend's friend hierarchy is being challenged, and friendship jealousy is likely to occur.

==== Attachment style ====
Research on romantic relationships suggests that there is indeed a link between [[Attachment theory|attachment style]] and jealousy. Specifically, individuals who demonstrate insecure attachments are more likely to experience romantic jealousy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Buunk |first=Bram P. |date=1997-12-01 |title=Personality, birth order and attachment styles as related to various types of jealousy |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=997–1006 |doi=10.1016/S0191-8869(97)00136-0 |issn=0191-8869}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chursina |first=Apollinaria V. |date=2023 |title=The Impact of Romantic Attachment Styles on Jealousy in Young Adults |url=https://psychologyinrussia.com/volumes/index.php?article=11698 |journal=Psychology in Russia: State of the Art |language=en |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=222–232 |doi=10.11621/pir.2023.0315 |issn=2074-6857 |pmc=10659228 |pmid=38024565}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Deng |first1=Min |last2=Tadesse |first2=Endale |last3=Khalid |first3=Sabika |last4=Zhang |first4=Weida |last5=Song |first5=Junrong |last6=Gao |first6=Chunhai |date=2023-08-24 |title=The influence of insecure attachment on undergraduates' jealousy: the mediating effect of self-differentiation |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=14 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1153866 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=10484705 |pmid=37691814}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rodriguez |first1=Lindsey M. |last2=DiBello |first2=Angelo M. |last3=Øverup |first3=Camilla S. |last4=Neighbors |first4=Clayton |date=2015 |title=The Price of Distrust: Trust, Anxious Attachment, Jealousy, and Partner Abuse |journal=Partner Abuse |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=298–319 |doi=10.1891/1946-6560.6.3.298 |issn=1946-6560 |pmc=5380380 |pmid=28386379}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rydell |first1=Robert J. |last2=Bringle |first2=Robert G. |date=2007-01-01 |title=Differentiating Reactive and Suspicious Jealousy |journal=Social Behavior and Personality|volume=35 |issue=8 |pages=1099–1114 |doi=10.2224/sbp.2007.35.8.1099}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sullivan |first=Kieran T. |date=2021-07-16 |title=Attachment Style and Jealousy in the Digital Age: Do Attitudes About Online Communication Matter? |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=12 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2021.678542 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=8322522 |pmid=34335391}}</ref> Although less well-established in the context of friendship, the association between attachment style and jealousy appears to persist. Specifically, individuals with anxious attachment styles are prone to higher levels of friendship jealousy than those with avoidant or secure attachment styles.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Murphy |first1=Tia Panfile |last2=Laible |first2=Deborah J. |last3=Augustine |first3=Mairin |last4=Robeson |first4=Lindsay |date=2015-09-03 |title=Attachment's Links With Adolescents' Social Emotions: The Roles of Negative Emotionality and Emotion Regulation |journal=The Journal of Genetic Psychology |language=en |volume=176 |issue=5 |pages=315–329 |doi=10.1080/00221325.2015.1072082 |pmid=26244914 |issn=0022-1325}}</ref> These associations might be explained by the relationship between anxious attachment and increased fear of [[Abandonment (emotional)|abandonment]] and [[Social rejection|rejection]], [[surveillance]] and reassurance-seeking behaviors, and a tendency to interpret social stimuli negatively.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=Gavin I. |last2=Rock |first2=Adam J. |last3=Clark |first3=Laura H. |last4=Murray-lyon |first4=Kerrin |date=2020-11-01 |title=Adult attachment, worry and reassurance seeking: Investigating the role of intolerance of uncertainty |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1111/cp.12218 |journal=Clinical Psychologist |language=en |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=294–305 |doi=10.1111/cp.12218 |issn=1328-4207}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Lorne |last2=Simpson |first2=Jeffry A. |last3=Boldry |first3=Jennifer |last4=Kashy |first4=Deborah A. |date=2005 |title=Perceptions of Conflict and Support in Romantic Relationships: The Role of Attachment Anxiety |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=88 |issue=3 |pages=510–531 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.88.3.510 |pmid=15740443 |issn=1939-1315}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nasiriavanaki |first1=Zahra |last2=Barbour |first2=Tracy |last3=Farabaugh |first3=Amy H. |last4=Fava |first4=Maurizio |last5=Holmes |first5=Avram J. |last6=Tootell |first6=Roger B. H. |last7=Holt |first7=Daphne J. |date=2021-01-01 |title=Anxious attachment is associated with heightened responsivity of a parietofrontal cortical network that monitors peri-personal space |journal=NeuroImage: Clinical |volume=30 |article-number=102585 |doi=10.1016/j.nicl.2021.102585 |doi-access=free |issn=2213-1582 |pmc=8024770 |pmid=33773165}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=DeWall |first1=C. Nathan |last2=Masten |first2=Carrie L. |last3=Powell |first3=Caitlin |last4=Combs |first4=David |last5=Schurtz |first5=David R. |last6=Eisenberger |first6=Naomi I. |date=2011-04-05 |title=Do neural responses to rejection depend on attachment style? An fMRI study |journal=Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=184–192 |pmc=3277372 |pmid=21467049 |doi=10.1093/scan/nsq107 |doi-access=free |issn=1749-5024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |journal=Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience |doi=10.1093/scan/nsu127 |doi-access=free |title=Attachment-security priming attenuates amygdala activation to social and linguistic threat |date=2015 |last1=Norman |first1=Luke |last2=Lawrence |first2=Natalia |last3=Iles |first3=Andrew |last4=Benattayallah |first4=Abdelmalek |last5=Karl |first5=Anke |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=832–839 |pmid=25326039 |pmc=4448028}}</ref>

==== Personality traits ====
Various [[personality]] traits have been shown to be associated with friendship jealousy. [[Aggression|Aggressive]] individuals, for example, are more likely to be jealous and possessive of their friends,<ref name=":2" /> a finding which is consistent with research on romantic jealousy.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hansen |first=G. K. |title=The psychology of jealousy and envy |publisher=Guilford Press |year=1991 |editor-last=Salovey |editor-first=P. |pages=211–230 |chapter=Jealousy: Its conceptualization, measurement, and integration with family stress theory}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stets |first1=Jan E. |last2=Pirog-Good |first2=Maureen A. |date=1987 |title=Violence in Dating Relationships |journal=Social Psychology Quarterly |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=237–246 |doi=10.2307/2786824 |jstor=2786824 |issn=0190-2725}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Sugarman |first=D. B. |title=Violence in dating relationships: Emerging social issues |publisher=Prager Publishers |year=1989 |editor-last=Pirog-Good |editor-first=M. A. |pages=3–32 |chapter=Dating violence: Prevalence, context, and risk markers |editor-last2=Stets |editor-first2=J. E.}}</ref> With regards to [[Big Five personality traits]], higher levels of [[neuroticism]],<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last1=Kokkinos |first1=Constantinos M. |last2=Kountouraki |first2=Magdalini |last3=Voulgaridou |first3=Ioanna |last4=Markos |first4=Angelos |date=2020-07-01 |title=Understanding the association between Big Five and relational aggression: The mediating role of social goals and friendship jealousy |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=160 |article-number=109946 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2020.109946 |issn=0191-8869}}</ref> and lower levels of [[Openness to experience|openness]]<ref name=":11" /> and [[conscientiousness]]<ref name=":10" /> have also been linked to increased friendship jealousy.

==== [[Biological sex|Sex]]/[[Gender]] ====
[[Woman|Women]] and [[girl]]s generally report higher levels of friendship jealousy than [[men]] and [[boy]]s do.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Deutz |first1=Marike H. F. |last2=Lansu |first2=Tessa A. M. |last3=Cillessen |first3=Antonius H. N. |date=February 2015 |title=Children's Observed Interactions With Best Friends: Associations With Friendship Jealousy and Satisfaction |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/sode.12080 |journal=Social Development |language=en |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=39–56 |doi=10.1111/sode.12080 |hdl=1874/309813 |issn=0961-205X|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kraft |first1=Caroline |last2=Mayeux |first2=Lara |date=March 2018 |title=Associations Among Friendship Jealousy, Peer Status, and Relational Aggression in Early Adolescence |journal=The Journal of Early Adolescence |language=en |volume=38 |issue=3 |pages=385–407 |doi=10.1177/0272431616670992 |issn=0272-4316}}</ref> This difference has been observed both in real-world and social media contexts, where women report more [[social media]] friendship jealousy relative to men.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Vaillancourt |first1=Tracy |last2=Brittain |first2=Heather |last3=Eriksson |first3=Mollie |last4=Krygsman |first4=Amanda |last5=Farrell |first5=Ann H. |last6=Davis |first6=Adam C. |last7=Volk |first7=Anthony A. |last8=Arnocky |first8=Steven |date=January 2024 |title=Social Media Friendship Jealousy |journal=Evolutionary Psychology |language=en |volume=22 |issue=1 |doi=10.1177/14747049231225738 |issn=1474-7049 |pmc=10787535 |pmid=38213116}}</ref> However, while women report greater friendship jealousy in best friendships, men appear to experience greater friendship jealousy when faced with the [[Prospective aspect|prospective]] loss of mere acquaintances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krems |first1=Jaimie Arona |last2=Williams |first2=Keelah E. G. |last3=Merrie |first3=Laureon A. |last4=Kenrick |first4=Douglas T. |last5=Aktipis |first5=Athena |date=2022-03-01 |title=Sex (similarities and) differences in friendship jealousy |journal=Evolution and Human Behavior |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=97–106 |bibcode=2022EHumB..43...97K |doi=10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2021.11.005 |issn=1090-5138|url=https://psyarxiv.com/gfpd8/ }}</ref>

Several explanations have been offered here. Girls tend to place importance on the exclusivity of their friendships,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Benenson |first=Joyce F. |date=1993 |title=Greater Preference among Females Than Males for Dyadic Interaction in Early Childhood |journal=Child Development |volume=64 |issue=2 |pages=544–555 |doi=10.2307/1131268 |jstor=1131268 |pmid=8477633 |issn=0009-3920}}</ref> seek emotional support from their friends,<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Rose |first1=Amanda J. |last2=Rudolph |first2=Karen D. |date=January 2006 |title=A review of sex differences in peer relationship processes: Potential trade-offs for the emotional and behavioral development of girls and boys |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=132 |issue=1 |pages=98–131 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.132.1.98 |issn=1939-1455 |pmc=3160171 |pmid=16435959}}</ref> expect [[loyalty]] and commitment from their friends,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sharabany |first1=Ruth |last2=Gershoni |first2=Ruth |last3=Hofman |first3=John E. |date=November 1981 |title=Girlfriend, boyfriend: Age and sex differences in intimate friendship |journal=Developmental Psychology |language=en |volume=17 |issue=6 |pages=800–808 |doi=10.1037/0012-1649.17.6.800 |issn=1939-0599}}</ref> and protect their [[Social group|social circles]] and activities from outsiders via social exclusion tactics<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berndt |first=Thomas J. |date=December 1982 |title=The Features and Effects of Friendship in Early Adolescence |journal=Child Development |volume=53 |issue=6 |pages=1447–1460 |doi=10.2307/1130071 |jstor=1130071}}</ref> more than boys do. Conversely, boys' social groups are often more sizable and shallow than girls' are.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maccoby |first=Eleanor E. |date=1990 |title=Gender and relationships: A developmental account |journal=American Psychologist |language=en |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=513–520 |doi=10.1037/0003-066X.45.4.513 |pmid=2186679 |issn=0003-066X}}</ref> Furthermore, girls seem to be more concerned with their relative hierarchical rank within their social groups<ref name=":13" /> – a quality which might increase the [[Salience (language)|salience]] of replacement threat in their friendships. Human females are also more likely to believe that when faced with a friendship rival, certain actions they take can successfully block prospective interference.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lavallee |first1=Kristen L. |last2=Parker |first2=Jeffrey G. |date=2019-01-16 |title=Beliefs about the controllability of social characteristics and children's jealous responses to outsiders' interference in friendship |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |article-number=e0209845 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0209845 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=6334908 |pmid=30650115|bibcode=2019PLoSO..1409845L }}</ref> Human females' closest same-sex friendships have also been shown to be more fragile than males', with females reporting proportionally higher instances of friendship [[Breakup|dissolution]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benenson |first1=Joyce F. |last2=Christakos |first2=Athena |date=July 2003 |title=The Greater Fragility of Females' Versus Males' Closest Same-Sex Friendships |url=https://srcd.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-8624.00596 |journal=Child Development |language=en |volume=74 |issue=4 |pages=1123–1129 |doi=10.1111/1467-8624.00596 |pmid=12938708 |issn=0009-3920|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==== Age ====
People's vulnerability to friendship jealousy varies over development. However, this variability does not follow a [[Linearity|linear]] trend; the likelihood of experiencing friendship jealousy appears to increase as children age,<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |last=Selman |first=Robert L. |title=The growth of interpersonal understanding: developmental and clinical analyses |date=1980 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-12-636450-7 |series=Developmental psychology series |location=New York}}</ref> decrease as children enter [[adolescence]], and increase again from middle adolescence onward.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6"/><ref name=":25">{{Cite journal |last1=Lavallee |first1=Kristen L. |last2=Parker |first2=Jeffrey G. |date=2009-08-01 |title=The Role of Inflexible Friendship Beliefs, Rumination, and Low Self-worth in Early Adolescents' Friendship Jealousy and Adjustment |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10802-009-9317-1 |journal=Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology |language=en |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=873–885 |doi=10.1007/s10802-009-9317-1 |pmid=19337827 |issn=1573-2835}}</ref> Although friendship jealousy has been shown to persist into [[young adult]]hood,<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Blomquist |first=Katrina Poetzl |date=2014 |title=Jealousy in Close Relationships Among Emerging Adults |url=https://dukespace.lib.duke.edu/items/77c553ac-4a55-433f-85a1-eeb2e7dd8ae3 |language=en}}</ref> more research is needed to identify trends in friendship jealousy over the lifespan.

==== Mental health ====
When individuals experience [[mental health]] challenges or [[Mental disorder|disorders]], such as [[loneliness]], self-esteem issues, [[Major depressive disorder|depression]], [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety]], and [[borderline personality disorder]], they may exhibit heightened sensitivity to relational dynamics. This can lead to increased monitoring and [[perception]] of potential threats to their relationships, making them more vulnerable to friendship jealousy.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":12" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Hwaheun |last2=Parker |first2=Jeffrey G. |last3=Walker Marciano |first3=Alisha R. |date=2017-09-01 |title=Interplay of self-esteem, emotion regulation, and parenting in young adolescents' friendship jealousy |journal=Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology |volume=52 |pages=170–180 |doi=10.1016/j.appdev.2017.06.007 |doi-access=free |issn=0193-3973}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stepp |first1=Stephanie D. |last2=Pilkonis |first2=Paul A. |last3=Hipwell |first3=Alison E. |last4=Loeber |first4=Rolf |last5=Stouthamer-Loeber |first5=Magda |date=August 2010 |title=Stability of Borderline Personality Disorder Features in Girls |journal=Journal of Personality Disorders |language=en |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=460–472 |doi=10.1521/pedi.2010.24.4.460 |issn=0885-579X |pmc=2920503 |pmid=20695806}}</ref> However, experiencing or expressing friendship jealousy is not inherently indicative of mental health disturbances, and can occur as a normal part of navigating social relationships.

== Behaviors associated with friendship jealousy ==

=== Friend guarding ===
[[File:Self-portrait Hesitating between the Arts of Music and Painting by Angelica Kauffmann.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|Rivals may compete for a friend's alliance by attempting to enhance their respective value.]]
In certain contexts, friendship jealousy may [[Motivation|motivate]] a host of [[behavior]]s aimed at countering the perceived threat, a [[phenomenon]] which is generally referred to as friend guarding.<ref name=":1" /> Friend guarding, similar in many respects to mate guarding in romantic relationships,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bleske-Rechek |first1=April |last2=Lighthall |first2=Melissa |date=March 2010 |title=Attractiveness and Rivalry in Women's Friendships with Women |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s12110-010-9081-5 |journal=Human Nature |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=82–97 |doi=10.1007/s12110-010-9081-5 |issn=1045-6767|url-access=subscription }}</ref> can manifest in a multitude of ways, and can occur with or without conscious premeditation.

==== Vigilance ====
When an individual perceives a third-party threat to their friendship, [[Vigilance (psychology)|vigilance]], monitoring, and surveilling efforts might increase. For example, a jealous individual may begin to pay more attention to how much time their friend is spending with a rival, make efforts to "catch" their friend spending time with a rival, and try to determine whether their friend values their friendship less than the friendship they have with a rival.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":15">Parker, J. G., Campbell, C., Lucas, A. (April, 2007). ''Individual differences in adolescents' behavioral and cognitive responses to jealousy and rival attractiveness among same-sex friends.'' Paper presented at the biennial meetings of the Society for Research in Child Development, Boston, MA.</ref>

==== Separation ====
Efforts to physically separate the friend and rival may also occur. For example, an individual may try to prevent their friend from attending events where the rival will be present, increase the spatial distance between the friend and rival (e.g., by sitting between them), interrupt conversations between the friend and rival, and interfere with plans the friend and rival have made to spend time together.<ref name=":1" />

==== Monopolization ====
A jealous individual may attempt to block opportunities for their friend to bond with a perceived rival by demanding so much of their friend's time and attention that the friend has little to no resources remaining to allocate to others.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":16">{{Cite thesis |last=Chung |first=Min-gi |title=Jealousy Responses in Same-Sex Friendship |date=2021 |publisher=UC San Diego |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/4232r210 |language=en}}</ref> In other words, by monopolizing their friend's resources, an individual makes it more difficult for a perceived rival to usurp them.

==== Self/commitment enhancement ====
Enhancing one's own physical, emotional, [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive]], or behavioral qualities, demonstrating high commitment to the friendship, accentuating [[love]], [[compassion]], and loyalty towards one's friend, and [[Deference|submitting]] to one's friend are examples of self/commitment enhancement as a friend guarding tactic.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":16" /> Such behaviors can be described as attempts to strengthen the existing bond, make the history or longevity of the friendship more salient, and inflate the value a friend places on the friendship in order to avoid being replaced.

==== Benefit provisioning ====
Benefit provisioning – although most often portrayed as a [[Mate guarding in humans|mate-retention tactic]] in the context of romantic or sexual relationships – refers to the offering of [[Tangibility|tangible]] or intangible benefits by the individual to the friend in an attempt to increase the value of the friendship. For example, a jealous individual might be more likely to do their friend a favor, present them with lavish [[gift]]s, offer abundant emotional support, or provide them with access to unique, positive experiences.<ref name=":16" />

==== Emotional manipulation ====
A jealous person might try to [[Manipulation (psychology)|manipulate]] their friend's emotions in a way that secures, reaffirms, or promotes their position in the larger friendship hierarchy. For example, a person might express feelings of dependence on their friend, display dejection when their friend spends substantial time hanging out with or talking about a rival, and try to make their friend feel [[Guilt (emotion)|guilty]] for fostering a close relationship with a rival.<ref name=":1" />

==== Possession signaling ====
Possession signaling refers to instances in which an individual engages in behaviors or communications that assert ownership or exclusivity over the friend who is the target of their friendship jealousy. Possession signaling tactics include introducing or otherwise labeling the friend as their "best friend," emphasizing the strength or closeness of the friendship to others, and strategically displaying one's level of closeness with the friend via social media posts, [[inside jokes]], and matching [[clothing]], [[tattoo]]s, [[jewellery]], etc.<ref name=":1" />

==== Jealousy induction ====
A person experiencing friendship jealousy might also attempt to make their friend reciprocate their jealousy by parading other friendships, making plans with others in front of their friend, exaggerating the closeness of other friendships, and so on.<ref name=":1" /> If an individual's attempts to make their friend jealous are successful, that friend is likely to also engage in friend-guarding tactics, thus reaffirming the individual's place in their friend's social network.

==== Competitor derogation ====
[[File:Gossip by Charles Haigh-Wood.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|left |Artwork depicting three women gossiping.]]
A jealous individual might speak negatively to their friend about a rival's physical, emotional, cognitive, or behavioral qualities, spread negative [[rumor]]s about a rival in hopes that they will reach the friend, and [[gossip]] or vent to their friend about a rival.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":15" /><ref name=":16" /><ref name=":17">{{Cite journal |last1=Culotta |first1=Carmen M. |last2=Goldstein |first2=Sara E. |date=2008-03-01 |title=Adolescents' Aggressive and Prosocial Behavior: Associations With Jealousy and Social Anxiety |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3200/GNTP.169.1.21-33 |journal=The Journal of Genetic Psychology |volume=169 |issue=1 |pages=21–33 |doi=10.3200/GNTP.169.1.21-33 |pmid=18476475 |issn=0022-1325|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krems |first1=Jaimie Arona |last2=Merrie |first2=Laureon A. |last3=Rodriguez |first3=Nina N. |last4=Williams |first4=Keelah E. G. |date=2024-09-01 |title=Venting makes people prefer—and preferentially support—us over those we vent about |journal=Evolution and Human Behavior |volume=45 |issue=5 |article-number=106608 |doi=10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2024.106608 |bibcode=2024EHumB..4506608K |issn=1090-5138|url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt62p3c9sj/qt62p3c9sj.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuttler |first1=Ami Flam |last2=Parker |first2=Jeffrey G. |last3=La Greca |first3=Annette M. (Annette Marie) |date=2002 |title=Developmental and Gender Differences in Preadolescents' Judgments of the Veracity of Gossip |journal=Merrill-Palmer Quarterly |language=en |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=105–132 |doi=10.1353/mpq.2002.0008 |issn=1535-0266}}</ref><ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Pronk |first1=Rhiarne E. |last2=Zimmer-Gembeck |first2=Melanie J. |date=March 2010 |title=It's "Mean," But What Does It Mean to Adolescents? Relational Aggression Described by Victims, Aggressors, and Their Peers |journal=Journal of Adolescent Research |language=en |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=175–204 |doi=10.1177/0743558409350504 |issn=0743-5584}}</ref> By making their rival less appealing, an individual might be able to decrease the level of threat the rival poses to their friendship.

==== Friend derogation ====
A jealous individual might also speak negatively to their ''rival'' about the mutual friend's physical, emotional, cognitive, or behavioral qualities, regardless of whether those flaws are genuine, [[exaggerated]], or falsified.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":15" /> Consequently, their friend will become less appealing, and the rival may no longer pursue the friendship.

==== Indirect competitor aggression ====
Some individuals may resort to indirect aggression in response to friendship jealousy. For example, they might attempt to make the rival feel uncomfortable or insecure in covert ways, such as by [[staring]] coldly at them, pretending not to hear them when they speak, excluding them from conversations, activities, or gatherings, and getting other friends to be [[Meanness|mean]] to them.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":15" /><ref name=":17" /><ref name=":19" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Owens |first1=Laurence |last2=Shute |first2=Rosalyn |last3=Slee |first3=Phillip |date=2000 |title=?Guess what I just heard!?: Indirect aggression among teenage girls in Australia |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1098-2337(2000)26:13.0.CO;2-C |journal=Aggressive Behavior |language=en |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=67–83 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1098-2337(2000)26:1<67::AID-AB6>3.0.CO;2-C |issn=0096-140X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The negative emotions experienced by the rival due to indirect aggression tactics may lead them to stop pursuing the friendship.

==== Friend punishment/threat ====
When the level of friendship jealousy experienced becomes too great to manage covertly, the individual may lash out at their friend, [[Yelling|yell]], become angry, display overt jealousy, give them the "[[cold shoulder]]," or threaten to end the friendship entirely.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":15" /> Hostile friend-guarding tactics such as this one are unlikely to benefit the individual's friendship.

==== Direct competitor aggression ====
[[File:Rebecca1917version.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|Extreme friendship jealousy may result in physical violence aimed at the perceived rival.]]
In its extreme form, friendship jealousy may motivate an individual to engage in aggressive [[confrontation]], [[bullying]], [[property destruction]], or even [[physical violence]] directed at their rival.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":15" /> The costs the rival might incur as a result of direct aggression may not be worth the value of the friend; consequently, the rival is likely to withdraw from the friendship. However, mitigating third-party threats in this way may come at the cost of the friendship itself.<ref name=":0" />

=== Bragging and boasting ===
Experiencing friendship jealousy might increase one's tendency to engage in bragging and boasting behaviors. For example, [[Boasting|bragging and boasting]] occurring shortly after a close friend has violated reciprocity norms due to third-party interference is a sign of friendship jealousy.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" /> An individual might brag and boast in order to [[Compensation (psychology)|compensate]] for recent damage to their self-esteem by making their accomplishments, abilities, and possessions more salient in an effort to [[self-soothe]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baumeister |first1=Roy F. |last2=Tice |first2=Dianne M. |date=June 1990 |title=Point-Counterpoints: Anxiety and Social Exclusion |journal=Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=165–195 |doi=10.1521/jscp.1990.9.2.165 |issn=0736-7236}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vohs |first1=Kathleen D. |last2=Heatherton |first2=Todd F. |date=2001 |title=Self-esteem and threats to self: Implications for self-construals and interpersonal perceptions |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=81 |issue=6 |pages=1103–1118 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.81.6.1103 |pmid=11761311 |issn=1939-1315}}</ref> or by signaling their superiority to others in order to increase their relative friendship value.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Leary |first1=Mark R. |chapter=The nature and function of self-esteem: Sociometer theory |date=2000 |title=Advances in Experimental Social Psychology |volume=32 |pages=1–62 |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1016/s0065-2601(00)80003-9 |isbn=978-0-12-015232-2 |last2=Baumeister |first2=Roy F.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Edward E. |title=Psychological perspectives on the self |last2=Pittman |first2=Thane S. |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |year=1982 |editor-last=Suls |editor-first=Jerry |volume=1 |location=Hillsdale, New Jersey |pages=232–262 |chapter=Toward a general theory of strategic self-presentation}}</ref>

=== Ignoring the issue/feigning indifference ===
Some individuals might ignore the issue altogether, attempt to suppress their jealousy, or feign [[Indifference (emotion)|indifference]] in order to avoid or mitigate discomfort, conflict, and threats to their self-esteem.<ref name=":15" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Salovey |first1=Peter |last2=Rodin |first2=Judith |date=March 1988 |title=Coping with Envy and Jealousy |journal=Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=15–33 |doi=10.1521/jscp.1988.7.1.15 |issn=0736-7236}}</ref>

=== Open communication ===
[[File:Uranie Alphonsine Colin-Libour -les 2 amies.jpg|thumb|left |A jealous friend might confront their feelings through open communication.]]
In sharp contrast with the aforementioned behaviors, an individual might outwardly and openly express the [[uncomfortable]] feelings they are experiencing to the close friend who is the target of their jealousy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bevan |first1=Jennifer L. |last2=Samter |first2=Wendy |date=March 2004 |title=Toward a broader conceptualization of jealousy in close relationships: Two exploratory studies |journal=Communication Studies |language=en |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=14–28 |doi=10.1080/10510970409388603 |issn=1051-0974}}</ref> They might advocate for themselves by asking their friend to explain their jealousy-eliciting behaviors, clarify their intentions, and provide them with greater emotional support, time allocation, or other expected benefits.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":16" /> As a result, the individual is likely to better understand the friend's perspective, secure increased benefits, and reduce their own jealousy.

== Friendship jealousy in non-human animals ==
The occurrence of friendship jealousy in non-human animals is an area of growing research interest. Many animals, such as [[chimpanzee]]s, [[monkey]]s, [[dolphin]]s, [[horse]]s, [[elephant]]s, and [[hyena]]s, are known to form long-lasting friendships.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Seyfarth |first1=Robert M. |last2=Cheney |first2=Dorothy L. |date=2012-01-10 |title=The Evolutionary Origins of Friendship |journal=Annual Review of Psychology |language=en |volume=63 |issue=1 |pages=153–177 |doi=10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100337 |pmid=21740224 |issn=0066-4308}}</ref> As such, it is unsurprising that non-human animals are also vulnerable to friendship jealousy. Various empirical research studies have reported evidence of jealousy in animals, including [[Titi monkey|Titi]] and [[Rhesus macaque|Rhesus]] monkeys, [[macaque]]s, and even [[dog]]s.
[[File:Common chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) grooming Kibale.jpg|thumb|Chimpanzees are known to form long-term friendships and show signs of jealousy.]]
Relevant [[Methodology|methodological]] approaches include using [[neuroimaging]] and behavioral [[observation]]s to [[Inference|infer]] animals' internal experiences of jealousy (e.g., increased activation of the [[amygdala]], and separation, monopolization, and direct competitor aggression tactics indicate possible jealousy evocation).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=Peter |last2=Prichard |first2=Ashley |last3=Spivak |first3=Mark |last4=Berns |first4=Gregory S. |date=2018-01-01 |title=Jealousy in dogs? Evidence from brain imaging |url=https://www.wellbeingintlstudiesrepository.org/animsent/vol3/iss22/1 |journal=Animal Sentience |language=en |volume=3 |issue=22 |doi=10.51291/2377-7478.1319 |issn=2377-7478|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Harris |first1=Christine R. |last2=Prouvost |first2=Caroline |date=2014-07-23 |title=Jealousy in Dogs |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=9 |issue=7 |article-number=e94597 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0094597 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=4108309 |pmid=25054800|bibcode=2014PLoSO...994597H}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maninger |first1=Nicole |last2=Mendoza |first2=Sally P. |last3=Williams |first3=Donald R. |last4=Mason |first4=William A. |last5=Cherry |first5=Simon R. |last6=Rowland |first6=Douglas J. |last7=Schaefer |first7=Thomas |last8=Bales |first8=Karen L. |date=2017-10-19 |title=Imaging, Behavior and Endocrine Analysis of "Jealousy" in a Monogamous Primate |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution |language=English |volume=5 |doi=10.3389/fevo.2017.00119 |doi-access=free |issn=2296-701X |pmc=5909987 |pmid=29682503}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rilling |first1=James K |last2=Sanfey |first2=Alan G |last3=Aronson |first3=Jessica A |last4=Nystrom |first4=Leigh E |last5=Cohen |first5=Jonathan D |date=2004-08-01 |title=The neural correlates of theory of mind within interpersonal interactions |journal=NeuroImage |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=1694–1703 |doi=10.1016/j.neuroimage.2004.04.015 |pmid=15275925 |issn=1053-8119}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Webb |first1=Christine E. |last2=Kolff |first2=Kayla |last3=Du |first3=Xuejing |last4=de Waal |first4=Frans |date=2020-12-01 |title=Jealous Behavior in Chimpanzees Elicited by Social Intruders |journal=Affective Science |language=en |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=199–207 |doi=10.1007/s42761-020-00019-5 |issn=2662-205X |pmc=9382973 |pmid=36042816}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Webb |first1=Christine E. |last2=de Waal |first2=Frans B. M. |date=2018-01-01 |title=Situating the study of jealousy in the context of social relationships |url=https://www.wellbeingintlstudiesrepository.org/animsent/vol3/iss22/22 |journal=Animal Sentience |language=en |volume=3 |issue=22 |doi=10.51291/2377-7478.1371 |issn=2377-7478|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zablocki-Thomas |first1=Pauline B. |last2=Rogers |first2=Forrest D. |last3=Bales |first3=Karen L. |date=2022-10-21 |title=Neuroimaging of human and non-human animal emotion and affect in the context of social relationships |journal=Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience |language=English |volume=16 |doi=10.3389/fnbeh.2022.994504 |doi-access=free |issn=1662-5153 |pmc=9633678 |pmid=36338883}}</ref> Chimpanzees, one of human's closest [[Genetics|genetic]] relatives,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Prüfer |first1=Kay |last2=Munch |first2=Kasper |last3=Hellmann |first3=Ines |last4=Akagi |first4=Keiko |last5=Miller |first5=Jason R. |last6=Walenz |first6=Brian |last7=Koren |first7=Sergey |last8=Sutton |first8=Granger |last9=Kodira |first9=Chinnappa |last10=Winer |first10=Roger |last11=Knight |first11=James R. |last12=Mullikin |first12=James C. |last13=Meader |first13=Stephen J. |last14=Ponting |first14=Chris P. |last15=Lunter |first15=Gerton |date=June 2012 |title=The bonobo genome compared with the chimpanzee and human genomes |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=486 |issue=7404 |pages=527–531 |bibcode=2012Natur.486..527P |doi=10.1038/nature11128 |issn=1476-4687 |pmc=3498939 |pmid=22722832}}</ref> have been found to engage in social exclusion and indirect competitor aggression tactics through [[coalition]]-building or by targeting rival's [[Reputation|reputations.]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goodall |first=Jane |date=January 1986 |title=Social rejection, exclusion, and shunning among the Gombe chimpanzees |journal=Ethology and Sociobiology |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3–4 |pages=227–236 |doi=10.1016/0162-3095(86)90050-6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gilby |first=Ian C. |date=2006-04-01 |title=Meat sharing among the Gombe chimpanzees: harassment and reciprocal exchange |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=71 |issue=4 |pages=953–963 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2005.09.009 |issn=0003-3472}}</ref> However, the majority of this research has investigated non-human animal displays of mate jealousy. More research is needed to evaluate predictors of and behaviors arising from friendship jealousy in various [[species]] across the animal kingdom.

== Consequences of friendship jealousy ==

=== Negative outcomes ===
Many modern cultures view jealousy in a negative light. As such, there exist social pressures which discourage people from both experiencing and expressing it.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last1=Argyle |first1=M. |last2=Henderson |first2=M. |last3=Furnham |first3=A. |date=June 1985 |title=The rules of social relationships |url=https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2044-8309.1985.tb00671.x |journal=British Journal of Social Psychology |language=en |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=125–139 |doi=10.1111/j.2044-8309.1985.tb00671.x |issn=0144-6665|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Furthermore, jealousy is generally seen as less acceptable in the context of friendships when compared to romantic or sexual relationships.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aune |first1=Krystyna Strzyzewski |last2=Comstock |first2=Jamie |date=August 1991 |title=Experience and Expression of Jealousy: Comparison between Friends and Romantics |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.2466/pr0.1991.69.1.315 |journal=Psychological Reports |language=en |volume=69 |issue=1 |pages=315–319 |doi=10.2466/pr0.1991.69.1.315 |pmid=1961815 |issn=0033-2941|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In research investigating the [[principle]]s which govern friendship, avoiding jealousy of a friend's other relationships has been identified as a basic rule.<ref name=":20" /> When an individual does experience friendship jealousy, they are likely to feel [[shame]] as a result of the social pressures and stigma associated with the emotion.

Internal consequences are not the only negative outcomes associated with friendship jealousy. Social demotion and [[Alienation from human society|alienation]], and, in some cases, complete friendship dissolution might also occur. For example, friendship jealousy might drive an individual to engage in certain behaviors (e.g., surveillance, manipulation, derogation, and physical violence), that have the potential to cause permanent destruction to their friendship.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Carson |first1=Christine L. |last2=Cupach |first2=William R. |date=September 2000 |title=Fueling the flames of the green-eyed monster: The role of ruminative thought in reaction to romantic jealousy |journal=Western Journal of Communication |language=en |volume=64 |issue=3 |pages=308–329 |doi=10.1080/10570310009374678 |issn=1057-0314}}</ref>

=== Positive outcomes ===
Although friendship jealousy is often perceived as a negative phenomenon, it can also produce positive effects. For example, expressing jealousy in a situationally appropriate, [[Prosocial behavior|prosocial]] way can signal to an individual that they are highly valued by their friend, to the extent that their friend cares deeply enough to preserve and [[Protection|protect]] the friendship from outside interference.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bringle |first1=Robert G |last2=Renner |first2=Patricia |last3=Terry |first3=Roger L |last4=Davis |first4=Susan |date=September 1983 |title=An analysis of situation and person components of jealousy |journal=Journal of Research in Personality |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=354–368 |doi=10.1016/0092-6566(83)90026-0 |issn=0092-6566}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Andersen |first1=Peter A. |last2=Eloy |first2=Sylvie V. |last3=Guerrero |first3=Laura K. |last4=Spitzberg |first4=Brian H. |date=June 1995 |title=Romantic jealousy and relational satisfaction: A look at the impact of jealousy experience and expression |journal=Communication Reports |language=en |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=77–85 |doi=10.1080/08934219509367613 |issn=0893-4215}}</ref> Experiencing jealousy can also motivate [[Personal development|self-improvement]] in the affected individual.<ref name=":21">{{Cite book |last1=Henninger |first1=N. E. |title=The positive side of negative emotions |last2=Harris |first2=C. R. |publisher=The Guilford Press |year=2014 |editor-last=Parrott |editor-first=W. G. |pages=76–97 |chapter=Can negative social emotions have positive consequences?: An examination of embarrassment, shame, guilt, jealousy, and envy.}}</ref>

Engaging in certain covert friend guarding behaviors may allow individuals to mitigate third-party threats whilst avoiding negative social consequences.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Björkqvist |first=Kaj |date=February 1994 |title=Sex differences in physical, verbal, and indirect aggression: A review of recent research |journal=Sex Roles |language=en |volume=30 |issue=3–4 |pages=177–188 |doi=10.1007/BF01420988 |issn=0360-0025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Xie |first1=Hongling |last2=Swift |first2=Dylan J. |last3=Cairns |first3=Beverley D. |last4=Cairns |first4=Robert B. |date=May 2002 |title=Aggressive Behaviors in Social Interaction and Developmental Adaptation: A Narrative Analysis of Interpersonal Conflicts During Early Adolescence |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9507.00195 |journal=Social Development |language=en |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=205–224 |doi=10.1111/1467-9507.00195 |issn=0961-205X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In jealous adolescents, for example, higher self-reported friendship jealousy has been found to be correlated with higher reports of [[Proactivity|proactive]] prosocial behavior.<ref name=":17" /> Proactive prosocial behavior differs from typical prosocial behavior due to its associations with aggressive cognitions and explicit motivations or objectives.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boxer |first1=Paul |last2=Tisak |first2=Marie S. |last3=Goldstein |first3=Sara E. |date=April 2004 |title=Is It Bad to Be Good? An Exploration of Aggressive and Prosocial Behavior Subtypes in Adolescence |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1023/B:JOYO.0000013421.02015.ef |journal=Journal of Youth and Adolescence |language=en |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=91–100 |doi=10.1023/B:JOYO.0000013421.02015.ef |issn=0047-2891|hdl=2027.42/45296 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In summary, strategically covert or situationally appropriate friendship jealousy behaviors can be effective in reaffirming one's friendship status and thwarting one's rivals.

== Relevant psychological frameworks ==

=== [[Developmental psychology]] ===

==== Stages of development ====
[[File:Young Girls Strike a Pose - Busua - Ghana (4737816187).jpg |thumb|upright=1.15|Young children may not be as likely to experience friendship jealousy.]]
An individual's vulnerability to jealousy is expected to fluctuate across the stages of development. For example, in early stages, individuals are expected to feel and express jealousy less frequently due to the level of socio-cognitive awareness required to perceive third-parties as potential threats to one's own friendships.<ref name=":14" /><ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last1=Selman |first1=R. L. |title=Making a friend in youth: Developmental theory and pair therapy. |last2=Schultz |first2=L. H. |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=1990}}</ref> According to [[Piaget's theory of cognitive development]], young children are [[Egocentrism|egocentric]] – meaning that they lack advanced social [[perspective-taking]] and [[theory of mind]], or the ability to understand that other people have their own [[cognition]]s, emotions, and perspectives.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Piaget |first=J. |title=The moral judgment of the child |publisher=Harcourt, Brace. |year=1932}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Premack |first1=David |last2=Woodruff |first2=Guy |date=December 1978 |title=Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0140525X00076512/type/journal_article |journal=Behavioral and Brain Sciences |language=en |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=515–526 |doi=10.1017/S0140525X00076512 |issn=0140-525X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wimmer |first=H |date=January 1983 |title=Beliefs about beliefs: Representation and constraining function of wrong beliefs in young children's understanding of deception |journal=Cognition |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=103–128 |doi=10.1016/0010-0277(83)90004-5 |pmid=6681741}}</ref> This feature of the preoperational stage of cognitive development thereby contributes to reduced friendship jealousy. Later, the frequency with which individuals experience friendship jealousy is expected to increase in late childhood, when socio-cognitive awareness is more developed, decrease as children enter adolescence, increase after middle adolescence, and abate after adolescence, when individuals' socio-cognitive capabilities mature.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":25" /><ref name=":14" /><ref name=":22" />

According to [[Erikson's stages of psychosocial development]], adolescents are faced with the crisis of [[Erikson's stages of psychosocial development#Fidelity: identity vs. role confusion (adolescence, 12–17 years)|identity vs. role confusion]], during which they seek to establish a stable sense of [[self]].<ref name=":23">{{Cite book |last=Erikson |first=E. H. |title=Childhood and society |publisher=W W Norton & Co. |year=1950}}</ref> The next stage, [[Erikson's stages of psychosocial development#Love: intimacy vs. isolation (early adulthood, 18–44 years)|intimacy vs. isolation]], begins in early adulthood, and is marked by the formation of long-term relationships, whether romantic or [[Platonic love|platonic]] in nature.<ref name=":23" /> Young adults might struggle to resist blending their [[Identity formation|identity]] with the identities of close-others, and when a third-party interferes with a close bond, the individual may isolate themselves and destroy the bonds which cause them [[Psychological pain|pain]].<ref name=":23" /> In alignment with this framework, friendship jealousy is likely to be especially prevalent and damaging during these developmental stages. It should be noted, however, that friendship jealousy may also play a pivotal role in later adulthood, as aging populations may need to rely more heavily on social bonds for physical and emotional assistance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lang |first=F. R. |date=2001-11-01 |title=Regulation of Social Relationships in Later Adulthood |journal=The Journals of Gerontology Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences |volume=56 |issue=6 |pages=P321–P326 |doi=10.1093/geronb/56.6.p321 |pmid=11682585 |issn=1079-5014}}</ref>

==== Self-determination theory ====
[[Self-determination theory]] posits that humans have three basic psychological needs that must be met in order to promote motivation, personal growth, and well-being: [[Self-determination theory#Autonomy|autonomy]], competence, and [[Self-determination theory#Relatedness|relatedness]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Deci |first1=Edward L. |last2=Ryan |first2=Richard M. |date=1980 |title=Self-determination Theory: When Mind Mediates Behavior |journal=The Journal of Mind and Behavior |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=33–43 |jstor=43852807 |issn=0271-0137}}</ref> Friendship rivals threaten the satisfaction of these needs; thus, jealousy may arise in order to motivate actions aimed at restoring essential need fulfillment.

==== Attachment theory ====
[[Attachment theory]], another major contribution of developmental psychology to the larger field,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bowlby |first=John |title=Attachment and loss. 1: Attachment |date=2003 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=978-0-465-00543-7 |edition=2. |location=New York}}</ref> is an additional highly relevant framework through which one can examine friendship jealousy. As explained above, people who have developed anxious attachment styles are more likely to experience friendship jealousy than people with other forms of attachment.<ref name=":10" /> This might be due to the fact that securely attached individuals perceive friendships as more stable, while avoidantly attached individuals may put significant conscious or unconscious effort into suppressing the jealousy they experience.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hazan |first1=Cindy |last2=Shaver |first2=Phillip |date=1987 |title=Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=511–524 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.52.3.511 |pmid=3572722 |issn=1939-1315}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Shaver |first1=P. R. |title=Handbook of emotion regulation |last2=Mikulincer |first2=M. |publisher=The Guilford Press |year=2007 |editor-last=Gross |editor-first=J. J. |pages=446–465}}</ref>

=== [[Social psychology]] ===

==== Comparison theories ====
[[Self-evaluation maintenance theory]]<ref name=":9" /> can help explain why people tend to experience greater jealousy when their rival outperforms them on particular dimensions.<ref name=":8" /> [[Social comparison theory]] similarly suggests that people evaluate themselves and their social prowess with respect to the performance, qualities, and capabilities of others.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Festinger |first=Leon |date=May 1954 |title=A Theory of Social Comparison Processes |journal=Human Relations |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=117–140 |doi=10.1177/001872675400700202 |issn=0018-7267}}</ref> When upward social comparisons are performed with a rival in mind, for example, replacement threat might increase, resulting in friendship jealousy.

==== Social exchange theories ====
According to [[social exchange theory]], [[social behavior]] is an exchange process whereby individuals interact with the expectation of receiving rewards or benefits.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Homans |first=George C. |date=May 1958 |title=Social Behavior as Exchange |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/222355 |journal=American Journal of Sociology |language=en |volume=63 |issue=6 |pages=597–606 |doi=10.1086/222355 |issn=0002-9602|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Furthermore, people seek to maximize their benefits and minimize their costs when engaging in [[Social relation|social interactions]] and forming social bonds; the most optimal relationship will be one in which benefits are mutually rewarding and costs are outweighed. [[Interdependence theory]], a type of social exchange theory, incorporates considerations of mutual dependence – in other words, to what extent the dyadic partners rely on one another.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rydell |first1=Robert J. |last2=McConnell |first2=Allen R. |last3=Bringle |first3=Robert G. |date=December 2004 |title=Jealousy and commitment: Perceived threat and the effect of relationship alternatives |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1475-6811.2004.00092.x |journal=Personal Relationships |language=en |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=451–468 |doi=10.1111/j.1475-6811.2004.00092.x |issn=1350-4126}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Thibaut |first1=J. W. |title=The social psychology of groups |last2=Kelley |first2=H. H. |publisher=John Wiley |year=1959}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kelley |first1=H. H. |title=Interpersonal relations: A theory of interdependence |last2=Thibaut |first2=J. |publisher=Wiley |year=1978 |location=New York}}</ref> Friendship jealousy, viewed through the lens of social exchange theory, is likely to occur when there is a discrepancy in the relative benefits allocated to the dyadic partners due to third-party interference.

==== Social identity theory ====
[[Social identity theory]] describes the social forces which drive an individual to claim membership in a particular social group, as well as the behaviors resulting from the establishment of discrete social groups.<ref name=":24">{{Cite book |last1=Tafjel |first1=H. |title=The social psychology of inter-group relations |last2=Turner |first2=J. C. |publisher=Brooks/Cole |year=1979 |editor-last=Austin |editor-first=W. G. |location=Monterey, CA |pages=33–47 |chapter=An integrative theory of inter-group conflict |editor-last2=Worchel |editor-first2=S.}}</ref> In accordance with this theory, friendships are most likely to be formed when potential dyadic partners share a central dimension of identity or are part of the same social group. In other words, there might exist [[Field theory (psychology)|social forces]] which motivate the formation of same-sex, same-race, and same-religion friendships, for example. However, once a friendship is formed, if the identity or group membership of a rival overlaps to a greater extent with the identity or group membership of one's friend, a cascade of consequences is likely to occur: replacement threat is increased, friendship jealousy is experienced, and the individual will engage in friendship jealousy behaviors.

=== [[Evolutionary psychology]] ===
[[File:Human Evolution Icon.png|thumb|Friendship jealousy might have evolved in humans as a tool to protect valuable alliances, maintain group cohesion, and ensure survival and reproductive fitness.]]

==== The alliance hypothesis ====
The alliance hypothesis for human friendship states that the evolutionary pressures faced by ancestral humans designed certain cognitive mechanisms which drive humans to identify and secure [[Alliance|allies]] in preparation for future conflict; thus, modern humans are motivated to find and make friends.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=DeScioli |first1=P. |title=Social judgment and decision making |last2=Kurzban |first2=R. |publisher=Psychology Press |year=2012 |editor-last=Krueger |editor-first=J. I. |pages=209–225 |chapter=The company you keep: Friendship decisions from a functional perspective}}</ref> Relatedly, researchers studying emotion from a [[Functional psychology|functional]] or [[Adaptationism|adaptationist]] standpoint argue that friendship jealousy arises when a valued friendship is threatened due to the risk of losing access to the [[Survival fitness|survival]] and [[reproductive fitness]] benefits they provide.<ref name=":21" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harris |first=Christine R. |date=May 2003 |title=A Review of Sex Differences in Sexual Jealousy, Including Self-Report Data, Psychophysiological Responses, Interpersonal Violence, and Morbid Jealousy |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1207/S15327957PSPR0702_102-128 |journal=Personality and Social Psychology Review |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=102–128 |doi=10.1207/S15327957PSPR0702_102-128 |pmid=12676643 |issn=1088-8683|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":18" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Salovey |first1=Peter |last2=Rodin |first2=Judith |date=October 1984 |title=Some antecedents and consequences of social-comparison jealousy |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=780–792 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.47.4.780 |issn=1939-1315}}</ref> The jealousy experienced then motivates the individual to leverage a suite of friend-retention tactics which have evolved alongside friendship jealousy due to their ability to effectively mitigate friendship threats and secure valuable resources.

==== Reciprocal altruism   ====
Many evolutionary psychologists believe that [[Reciprocal altruism in humans|reciprocal altruism]] evolved in humans because individuals who help others are more likely to receive future reciprocation, thus increasing their survival and reproductive fitness.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Trivers |first=Robert L. |date=1971 |title=The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=35–57 |doi=10.1086/406755 |jstor=2822435 |issn=0033-5770}}</ref> Reciprocity, it is argued, ensures the strength and maintenance of alliances; perceived imbalances or reciprocity violations can lead to jealousy. Social identity theory is also relevant here, since preferential in-group treatment has several evolutionary implications.<ref name=":24" /> For example, friends and family are part of a person's [[In-group and out-group|in-group]]; thus, individuals might be motivated to extend preferential treatment, protection, and benefit provisioning to the offspring of their friends. By doing so, the individual is able to ensure future reciprocity for themselves and their own [[offspring]].

==== Group selection theory ====
Group selection theory suggests that certain qualities or traits might evolve not necessarily for the benefit of the individual, but to benefit the overall group that individual belongs to – even at the individual's direct expense.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=D S |date=January 1975 |title=A theory of group selection |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=143–146 |doi=10.1073/pnas.72.1.143 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=432258 |pmid=1054490|bibcode=1975PNAS...72..143W }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=David Sloan |last2=Wilson |first2=Edward O. |date=December 2007 |title=Rethinking the Theoretical Foundation of Sociobiology |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/522809 |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology |language=en |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=327–348 |doi=10.1086/522809 |pmid=18217526 |issn=0033-5770|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Although friendship jealousy has the potential to negatively impact the [[emotional well-being]] and social status of the individual, it might have evolved to protect and maintain the larger structure of the social group. A single ancestral human might have been able to mitigate threats to group cohesion resulting from the strengthening of unprecedented social bonds by engaging in jealousy behaviors, even if the consequences of those behaviors were detrimental to their own survival and reproductive fitness.

==== Costly signaling theory ====
[[Costly signaling theory in evolutionary psychology|Costly signaling theory]] – which states that individuals may engage in behaviors that are costly in order to signal their [[Authenticity (philosophy)|authenticity]] and commitment<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zahavi |first=Amotz |date=1975-09-01 |title=Mate selection—A selection for a handicap |journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=205–214 |doi=10.1016/0022-5193(75)90111-3 |pmid=1195756 |bibcode=1975JThBi..53..205Z |issn=0022-5193}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Grafen |first=Alan |date=1990-06-21 |title=Biological signals as handicaps |journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology |volume=144 |issue=4 |pages=517–546 |doi=10.1016/S0022-5193(05)80088-8 |pmid=2402153 |bibcode=1990JThBi.144..517G |issn=0022-5193}}</ref> – offers a framework through which we can examine displays of friendship jealousy. Because friendship jealousy and its associated behaviors carry negative consequences, such as social stigma, resource expenditure, emotional vulnerability, and friendship dissolution, people are unlikely to feign the experience of jealousy without genuine concern for the friendship at hand. As a result, friends are more likely to believe the individual's experience is [[Sincerity|sincere]] and respond positively to it, and the individual is able to effectively and accurately signal the value they place on the friendship. In alignment with this framework, the more costly the signal, the more valuable the friendship is likely to be to the individual. Thus, friendship jealousy may be understood as an effective [[tool]] used to preserve social bonds.
