======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: AI anthropomorphism
======================================================================

{{Short description|Attribution of human traits to AI}}
'''AI anthropomorphism''' is the attribution of [[Humanism|human-like]] feelings, mental states, and behavioral characteristics to [[artificial intelligence]] systems. Factors related to the user of the AI – such as culture, age, education, gender, and personality traits – are also important determinants of the strength of anthropomorphic effects.

Since the earliest days of AI development, humans have interpreted machine outputs through [[Anthropomorphism|anthropomorphic]] frameworks, but the recent emergence of generative AI has amplified these tendencies. Terms such as [[machine learning|learning]], [[natural language understanding|understanding]], [[reasoning model|reasoning]], [[Prompt engineering#Chain-of-thought|thinking]], [[Hallucination (artificial intelligence)|hallucinating]] and [[AI planning|planning]] are frequently used in AI research to describe capabilities of AI systems, without necessarily implying [[Artificial consciousness|consciousness]], [[sentience]], human-like [[cognition]], or understanding in a stronger philosophical sense.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mitchell |first1=Melanie |last2=Krakauer |first2=David C. |title=The debate over understanding in AI's large language models |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=120 |issue=13 |article-number=e2215907120 |date=2023 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2215907120 |doi-access=free |pmid=36943882 |pmc=10068812 |arxiv=2210.13966 |bibcode=2023PNAS..12015907M }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shardlow |first1=Matthew |last2=Przybyła |first2=Piotr |date=2024 |title=Deanthropomorphising NLP: Can a language model be conscious? |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=19 |issue=12 |article-number=e0307521 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0307521 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=11617003 |pmid=39631034 |arxiv=2211.11483 |bibcode=2024PLoSO..1907521S }}</ref>

In research and engineering, there is a distinction between anthropomorphism and anthropomorphic design. The former is an innate human tendency toward non-human entities. The latter is the scientific community or commercial effort to “design anthropomorphism”.<ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Bao |first1=Zhuolan |last2=Chen |first2=Jiashu |last3=Luo |first3=Yunzhong |last4=Reani |first4=Manuele |date=2022-07-04 |title=Convincing or Odd: Anthropomorphic Design Cues in Chatbots |url=https://aisel.aisnet.org/pacis2022/255 |journal=PACIS 2022 Proceedings}}</ref> Such a design can involve the manipulation of cues, including AI appearance, behaviour and language.<ref name=":19" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Seeger |first1=Anna-Maria |last2=Pfeiffer |first2=Jella |last3=Heinzl |first3=Armin |date=2021-01-01 |title=Texting with Humanlike Conversational Agents: Designing for Anthropomorphism |url=https://aisel.aisnet.org/jais/vol22/iss4/8 |journal=Journal of the Association for Information Systems |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=931–967 |doi=10.17705/1jais.00685 |issn=1536-9323}}</ref> Contemporary AI systems today can generate extremely human-like outputs and are often designed specifically to do so, meaning that their anthropomorphic effects can be especially powerful. 

In some cases, anthropomorphism is accompanied with explicit beliefs that AI systems are capable of empathy, goodwill, understanding, or consciousness.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Marcus |first=Gary F. |title=Rebooting AI: building artificial intelligence we can trust |date=2019 |publisher=Pantheon Books |others=Ernest Davis |isbn=978-1-5247-4825-8 |edition=First |location=New York}}</ref>

== Background ==

=== In early AIs ===
Views of artificial agents possessing a human-like intelligence have existed since the early development of computers in the mid-1900s. The use of the human mind as a metaphor for understanding the workings of machine systems was prevalent among researchers in the early days of computer science, with multiple influential works widely distributing the idea of intelligent machines.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wiener |first=Norbert |url=https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/4581/Cybernetics-or-Control-and-Communication-in-the |title=Cybernetics or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine |date=2019-10-08 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-35590-2 |language=en |doi=10.7551/mitpress/11810.001.0001}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McCulloch |first1=Warren S. |last2=Pitts |first2=Walter |date=1943-12-01 |title=A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity |journal=The Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=115–133 |doi=10.1007/BF02478259 |bibcode=1943BMaB....5..115M |issn=1522-9602}}</ref> Among the most widely cited papers of this period was [[Alan Turing]]'s "[[Computing Machinery and Intelligence]]" in which he introduced the [[Turing test|Turing Test]], stating that a machine was intelligent if it could produce conversation that was indistinguishable from that of a human.<ref name="Turing1950">{{Cite journal |last=Turing |first=A. M. |author-link=Alan Turing |date=1950-10-01 |title=I.—Computing Machinery and Intelligence |url=https://academic.oup.com/mind/article/LIX/236/433/986238 |journal=Mind |language=en |volume=LIX |issue=236 |pages=433–460 |doi=10.1093/mind/LIX.236.433 |issn=1460-2113|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These academic works in the 1940s and 1950s gave early credibility to the idea that machine workings could be thought of similarly to human minds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Natale |first1=Simone |last2=Ballatore |first2=Andrea |date=2020-02-01 |title=Imagining the thinking machine: Technological myths and the rise of artificial intelligence |journal=Convergence |language=EN |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=3–18 |doi=10.1177/1354856517715164 |hdl=2318/1768454 |issn=1354-8565|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The public quickly came to view artificial systems similarly, with often exaggerated conceptions of the capabilities of early machines.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Martin |first=C. Dianne |date=1993-04-01 |title=The myth of the awesome thinking machine |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/255950.153587 |journal=Commun. ACM |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=120–133 |doi=10.1145/255950.153587 |issn=0001-0782}}</ref> Among the most well-known demonstrations of this was through the chatbot [[ELIZA]] designed by [[Joseph Weizenbaum]] in 1966. ELIZA responded to user inputs with a rudimentary text-processing approach that could not be considered anything resembling true understanding of the inputs, yet users, even when operating with full conscious knowledge of ELIZA's limitations, often began to ascribe motivation and understanding to the program's output (see [[ELIZA effect]]).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Suchman |first=Lucille Alice |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AJ_eBJtHxmsC&q=Suchman+Plans+and+Situated+Actions |title=Plans and Situated Actions: The Problem of Human-Machine Communication |date=1987-11-26 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-33739-7 |language=en}}</ref> Weizenbaum later wrote, "I had not realized ... that extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Weizenbaum |first=Joseph |title=Computer power and human reason: from judgment to calculation |date=1976 |publisher=Freeman |isbn=978-0-7167-0464-5 |location=San Francisco}}</ref>

Comparisons between the intellectual capabilities of artificial intelligence and human intelligence were continually intensified by the attempts of computer scientists to develop machines that could perform human tasks at a level equal to or better than humans. A symbolic turning point was achieved in 1997, when [[IBM]]'s chess supercomputer [[Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov|Deep Blue defeated then-world champion Garry Kasparov]] in a highly publicized six-game match.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Team (CHESScom) |first=Chess com |date=2018-10-01 |title=Kasparov vs. Deep Blue {{!}} The Match That Changed History |url=https://www.chess.com/article/view/deep-blue-kasparov-chess |access-date=2025-10-30 |website=Chess.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The defeat of a human by a machine for the first time in chess – a game viewed as a canonical example of human intellect – and the media attention surrounding the match led to a significant shift, where views of parallels between human and artificial intelligence moved from abstract speculation to being concretely demonstrated.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Greenemeier |first=Larry |title=20 Years after Deep Blue: How AI Has Advanced Since Conquering Chess |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/20-years-after-deep-blue-how-ai-has-advanced-since-conquering-chess/ |access-date=2025-11-02 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> A similar achievement was reached in the board game [[Go (game)|Go]] in 2017, when the program [[AlphaGo]] defeated world top-ranked [[Ke Jie]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=France-Presse |first=Agence |date=2017-05-23 |title=World's best Go player flummoxed by Google's 'godlike' AlphaGo AI |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2017/may/23/alphago-google-ai-beats-ke-jie-china-go |access-date=2025-11-02 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Large language models ===
The [[AI boom]] of the 2020s brought about the widespread emergence of [[Generative artificial intelligence|generative AI]]; in particular, chatbots such as [[ChatGPT]], [[Google Gemini|Gemini]], and [[Claude (language model)|Claude]] based on [[large language model]]s (LLMs) have become increasingly pervasive in everyday society. These systems are notable for the fact that they are able to respond to a wide range of prompts across contexts while producing strikingly human-like outputs – research has shown that humans are often unable to distinguish human-generated text from AI-generated text, and modern AI chatbots have formally been shown to pass the Turing test.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Jakesch |first1=Maurice |last2=Hancock |first2=Jeffrey T. |last3=Naaman |first3=Mor |date=2023-03-14 |title=Human heuristics for AI-generated language are flawed |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=120 |issue=11 |article-number=e2208839120 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2208839120 |doi-access=free |pmc=10089155 |pmid=36881628 |arxiv=2206.07271 |bibcode=2023PNAS..12008839J }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mei |first1=Qiaozhu |last2=Xie |first2=Yutong |last3=Yuan |first3=Walter |last4=Jackson |first4=Matthew O. |date=2024-02-27 |title=A Turing test of whether AI chatbots are behaviorally similar to humans |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=121 |issue=9 |article-number=e2313925121 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2313925121 |doi-access=free |pmc=10907317 |pmid=38386710 |bibcode=2024PNAS..12113925M }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Jones |first1=Cameron R. |title=Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test |date=2025-03-31 |eprint=2503.23674 |last2=Bergen |first2=Benjamin K. |class=cs.CL }}</ref> As such, the anthropomorphic effects of AI are more powerful than ever.<ref name=":15" /> Given that LLMs have brought AI into the technological mainstream, considerable scientific effort has been devoted in recent years to understand existing and potential ramifications of AI in the public sphere; the prevalence and effects of anthropomorphism is one of those domains where much of this effort has been directed.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":16" />

== Current anthropomorphic attributions ==

=== In the general public ===
Surveys have shown that a substantial portion of the public attributes human-like qualities to AI. In one sample of U.S. adults from 2024, two-thirds of people believed that ChatGPT is possibly conscious on some level,<ref name=":14" /> though other research has shown that the public still views the likelihood itself of [[AI consciousness]] as comparatively low.<ref name=":14" /><ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Dreksler |first1=Noemi |title=Subjective Experience in AI Systems: What Do AI Researchers and the Public Believe? |date=2025-06-16 |eprint=2506.11945 |last2=Caviola |first2=Lucius |last3=Chalmers |first3=David |last4=Allen |first4=Carter |last5=Rand |first5=Alex |last6=Lewis |first6=Joshua |last7=Waggoner |first7=Philip |last8=Mays |first8=Kate |last9=Sebo |first9=Jeff |class=cs.CY }}</ref> Another study conducted in 2025 found that women, people of color, and older individuals were most likely to anthropomorphize AI, as well as that – in general – humans view AIs as warm and competent, and anthropomorphic attributions to AI had increased by 34% in the past year.<ref name=":15">{{cite journal |last1=Cheng |first1=Myra |title=Metaphors of AI indicate that people increasingly perceive AI as warm and human-like |date=2026 |arxiv=2501.18045 |last2=Lee |first2=Angela Y. |last3=Rapuano |first3=Kristina |last4=Niederhoffer |first4=Kate |last5=Liebscher |first5=Alex |last6=Hancock |first6=Jeffrey |journal=Communications Psychology |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=8 |doi=10.1038/s44271-025-00376-6  |doi-access=free|pmid=41514014 |pmc=12808644 }}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|reason=Non-peer reviewed source on a preprint repository (generally inappropriate to cite), partially co-authored by two AI company executives|date=December 2025}} A [[YouGov]] poll reported that 46% of Americans believe that people should display politeness to AI chatbots by saying "please" and "thank you", demonstrating the application of social norms to AI.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Do you think people should be polite to AI chatbots, for example by saying "please" and "thank you"? {{!}} Daily Question |url=https://today.yougov.com/topics/technology/survey-results/daily/2025/04/30/dcf71/2 |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=today.yougov.com |language=en-us}}</ref> These beliefs extend to behavior, where majorities of AI users claim to always be polite to chatbots; of those who behave politely, most say they do so simply because it is the "nice" thing to do.<ref>{{Cite web |author1=Hamish Hector |date=2025-02-20 |title=Are you polite to ChatGPT? Here's where you rank among AI chatbot users |url=https://www.techradar.com/computing/artificial-intelligence/are-you-polite-to-chatgpt-heres-where-you-rank-among-ai-chatbot-users |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=TechRadar |language=en}}</ref>

In many recent cases, humans have developed robust interpersonal bonds with AI systems. For example: users of social chatbots like [[Replika]] and [[Character.ai]] have been documented to fall in love with the AIs, or to otherwise treat the AIs as intimate companions,<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Roose |first1=Kevin |date=2024-10-23 |title=Can A.I. Be Blamed for a Teen's Suicide? (Published 2024) |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/23/technology/characterai-lawsuit-teen-suicide.html |access-date=2025-11-14 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Man Dies by Suicide After Conversations with AI Chatbot That Became His 'Confidante,' Widow Says |url=https://people.com/human-interest/man-dies-by-suicide-after-ai-chatbot-became-his-confidante-widow-says/ |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=People.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-22 |title=S6, Episode 3: Love in Time of Replika (April 25th, 2023) |url=https://hiphination.org/season-6-episodes/s6-episode-3-love-in-time-of-replika/ |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=Hi-Phi Nation |language=en}}</ref> and it has become increasingly common for individuals to use LLMs like ChatGPT as therapists.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Quiroz-Gutierrez |first=Marco |title=People are increasingly turning to ChatGPT for affordable on-demand therapy, but licensed therapists say there are dangers many aren't considering |url=https://fortune.com/2025/06/01/ai-therapy-chatgpt-characterai-psychology-psychiatry/ |access-date=2025-11-14 |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref> Chatbots are able to produce responses deeply attuned to users, as they are often designed to maximize agreeableness and mirror users' emotions; this can create compelling illusions of intimacy.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Chu |first1=Minh Duc |title=Illusions of Intimacy: Emotional Attachment and Emerging Psychological Risks in Human-AI Relationships |date=2025-06-11 |eprint=2505.11649 |last2=Gerard |first2=Patrick |last3=Pawar |first3=Kshitij |last4=Bickham |first4=Charles |last5=Lerman |first5=Kristina |class=cs.SI }}</ref>

=== In the research community ===
In many cases, even AI researchers anthropomorphize AI systems in some capacity. Among the most extreme and well-publicized of these instances occurred in 2022, when engineer Blake Lemoine publicly claimed that [[Google]]'s LLM [[LaMDA]] was conscious.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-06-11 |title=The Google engineer who thinks the company's AI has come to life |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2022/06/11/google-ai-lamda-blake-lemoine/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Lemoine published the transcript of a conversation he had had with LaMDA regarding self identity and morality which he claimed was evidence of its sentience; he asserted that LaMDA was "a person" as defined by the [[Constitution of the United States|United States Constitution]] and compared its mental capability to that of a 7- or 8-year-old.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Levy |first=Steven |title=Blake Lemoine Says Google's LaMDA AI Faces 'Bigotry' |url=https://www.wired.com/story/blake-lemoine-google-lamda-ai-bigotry/ |access-date=2025-11-10 |magazine=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> Lemoine's claims were widely dismissed by the scientific community and by Google itself, which described Lemoine's conclusions as "wholly unfounded" and fired him on the grounds that he had violated policies "to safeguard product information".<ref>{{Cite news |title=Google fires software engineer who claimed its AI chatbot is sentient |url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/google-fires-software-engineer-who-claimed-its-ai-chatbot-is-sentient-2022-07-23/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240921220914/https://www.reuters.com/technology/google-fires-software-engineer-who-claimed-its-ai-chatbot-is-sentient-2022-07-23/ |archive-date=2024-09-21 |access-date=2025-11-10 |work=Reuters |language=en-US}}</ref>

It is much more common that AI researchers unintentionally imply humanness of AI through the ordinary use of anthropomorphic language to describe nonhuman agents.<ref name=":11" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Proudfoot |first=Diane |date=2011-04-01 |title=Anthropomorphism and AI: Turingʼs much misunderstood imitation game |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000437021100018X |journal=Artificial Intelligence |series=Special Review Issue |volume=175 |issue=5 |pages=950–957 |doi=10.1016/j.artint.2011.01.006 |issn=0004-3702|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This kind of language, which [[Daniel Dennett]] coined the "[[intentional stance]]",<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dennett |first=Daniel |title=The Intentional Stance |publisher=MIT Press |year=1987}}</ref> is very common in everyday life in a variety of different contexts (e.g., "My computer doesn't want to turn on today"). For AI agents that may actually appear to very closely replicate some human abilities, however, the casual use of such anthropomorphic language in research has been scrutinized for being potentially misleading to the public. As early as 1976, [[Drew McDermott]] criticized the research community for the use of "wishful mnemonics", where AIs were referred to with terms like "understand" and "learn".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McDermott |first=Drew |date=1976-04-01 |title=Artificial intelligence meets natural stupidity |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1045339.1045340 |journal= ACM SIGART Bulletin|issue=57 |pages=4–9 |doi=10.1145/1045339.1045340 |issn=0163-5719|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In the LLM era, these criticisms have further intensified, with the negative effects of AI anthropomorphism in the public posing an especially salient danger given the elevated accessibility of modern AI.<ref name=":11" /><ref name=ShanahanM>{{cite arXiv|last=Shanahan |first=Murray |title=Talking About Large Language Models |date=2023-02-17 |class=cs.CL |eprint=2212.03551 }}</ref>

In some cases, the use of anthropomorphic language for AI is not unintentional, but is willfully used by researchers in order to promote better understanding of the brain – the idea being that, as AI can be functionally similar in some ways to the human brain, we may gain new insights and ideas from treating AI as a kind of model of the brain's workings.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Prescott |first1=Tony J. |chapter=The Synthetic Psychology of the Self |date=2019 |title=Cognitive Architectures |pages=85–104 |editor-last=Aldinhas Ferreira |editor-first=Maria Isabel  |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-97550-4_7 |isbn=978-3-319-97550-4 |last2=Camilleri |first2=Daniel |editor2-last=Silva Sequeira |editor2-first=João |editor3-last=Ventura |editor3-first=Rodrigo}}</ref> In particular, [[deep neural network]]s (DNNs) are often explicitly compared to the human brain, and significant advances in DNN research have stirred considerable enthusiasm about the ability of AI to emulate the human abilities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Silver |first1=David |last2=Schrittwieser |first2=Julian |last3=Simonyan |first3=Karen |last4=Antonoglou |first4=Ioannis |last5=Huang |first5=Aja |last6=Guez |first6=Arthur |last7=Hubert |first7=Thomas |last8=Baker |first8=Lucas |last9=Lai |first9=Matthew |last10=Bolton |first10=Adrian |last11=Chen |first11=Yutian |last12=Lillicrap |first12=Timothy |last13=Hui |first13=Fan |last14=Sifre |first14=Laurent |last15=van den Driessche |first15=George |date=October 2017 |title=Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24270 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=550 |issue=7676 |pages=354–359 |doi=10.1038/nature24270 |pmid=29052630 |bibcode=2017Natur.550..354S |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Caution has been urged in this domain as well, however; the use of anthropomorphic language can mask important differences that fundamentally distinguish AI from human intelligence.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Marcus |first=Gary |title=Deep Learning: A Critical Appraisal |date=2018-01-03 |class=cs.AI |eprint=1801.00631 }}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Watson |first=David |date=2019-09-01 |title=The Rhetoric and Reality of Anthropomorphism in Artificial Intelligence |journal=Minds and Machines |language=en |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=417–440 |doi=10.1007/s11023-019-09506-6 |issn=1572-8641|doi-access=free }}</ref> When it comes to DNNs, for example, it has been pointed out that they are still structurally quite different from the human brain, with much of what we know about human neurons not having been incorporated.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ullman |first=Shimon |date=2019-02-15 |title=Using neuroscience to develop artificial intelligence |url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.aau6595 |journal=Science |language=EN |volume=363 |issue=6428 |pages=692–693 |doi=10.1126/science.aau6595 |pmid=30765552 |bibcode=2019Sci...363..692U |issn=0036-8075 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017165617/https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.aau6595 |archive-date=2022-10-17|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It has also been argued that DNNs are less efficient and less durable in generating correct outputs than the human brain, given that they require significantly more training data than the brain and can sometimes be easily "fooled" by perturbations in input data.<ref name=":12" /><ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Goodfellow |first1=Ian J. |title=Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples |date=2015-03-24 |last2=Shlens |first2=Jonathon |last3=Szegedy |first3=Christian |class=stat.ML |eprint=1412.6572 }}</ref> Given these fundamental differences, research focuses toward making AI as similar as possible to biological intelligence (which may be promoted by using anthropomorphic language) could hinder future AI development by limiting the proliferation of new theoretical and operational frameworks.<ref name=":11" />

== Agent factors ==

=== Physical factors ===

==== Appearance ====
In general, AIs that appear more human-like will be subject to more anthropomorphic attributions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Manzi |first1=Federico |last2=Massaro |first2=Davide |last3=Di Lernia |first3=Daniele |last4=Maggioni |first4=Mario A. |last5=Riva |first5=Giuseppe |last6=Marchetti |first6=Antonella |date=May 2021 |title=Robots Are Not All the Same: Young Adults' Expectations, Attitudes, and Mental Attribution to Two Humanoid Social Robots |url=https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/full/10.1089/cyber.2020.0162 |journal=Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking |volume=24 |issue=5 |pages=307–314 |doi=10.1089/cyber.2020.0162 |pmid=33181030 |issn=2152-2715|hdl=10807/251256 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Manzi |first1=Federico |last2=Peretti |first2=Giulia |last3=Di Dio |first3=Cinzia |last4=Cangelosi |first4=Angelo |last5=Itakura |first5=Shoji |last6=Kanda |first6=Takayuki |last7=Ishiguro |first7=Hiroshi |last8=Massaro |first8=Davide |last9=Marchetti |first9=Antonella |date=2020-09-30 |title=A Robot Is Not Worth Another: Exploring Children's Mental State Attribution to Different Humanoid Robots |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=11 |article-number=2011 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2020.02011 |pmid=33101099 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078|pmc=7554578 }}</ref> Effect of appearance is most pronounced when it comes to the face of the AI;<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yee |first1=Nick |last2=Bailenson |first2=Jeremy N |last3=Rickertsen |first3=Kathryn |chapter=A meta-analysis of the impact of the inclusion and realism of human-like faces on user experiences in interfaces |date=2007-04-29 |title=Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1240624.1240626 |series=CHI '07 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1145/1240624.1240626 |isbn=978-1-59593-593-9}}</ref> the most important components for anthropomorphism in a robot's design are the eyes, nose, and mouth, where the number of human-like features in the face is correlated with the level of anthropomorphic attribution.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Dubois-Sage |first1=Marion |last2=Jacquet |first2=Baptiste |last3=Jamet |first3=Frank |last4=Baratgin |first4=Jean |date=2023-07-28 |title=We Do Not Anthropomorphize a Robot Based Only on Its Cover: Context Matters too! |journal=Applied Sciences |language=en |volume=13 |issue=15 |page=8743 |doi=10.3390/app13158743 |doi-access=free |issn=2076-3417 }}</ref> The humanness of a robot's appearance is usually associated with more positive feelings toward the robot,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zanatto |first1=Debora |last2=Patacchiola |first2=Massimiliano |last3=Cangelosi |first3=Angelo |last4=Goslin |first4=Jeremy |date=2020-01-01 |title=Generalisation of Anthropomorphic Stereotype |journal=International Journal of Social Robotics |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=163–172 |doi=10.1007/s12369-019-00549-4 |issn=1875-4805 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krach |first1=Sören |last2=Hegel |first2=Frank |last3=Wrede |first3=Britta |last4=Sagerer |first4=Gerhard |last5=Binkofski |first5=Ferdinand |last6=Kircher |first6=Tilo |date=2008-07-09 |title=Can Machines Think? Interaction and Perspective Taking with Robots Investigated via fMRI |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=3 |issue=7 |article-number=e2597 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0002597 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=2440351 |pmid=18612463 |bibcode=2008PLoSO...3.2597K }}</ref> though highly human-like appearance can sometimes trigger feelings of strangeness and unease, known as the [[uncanny valley]] phenomenon.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mori |first1=Masahiro |last2=MacDorman |first2=Karl |last3=Kageki |first3=Norri |title=The Uncanny Valley [From the Field] |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/254060168 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241109040217/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/254060168_The_Uncanny_Valley_From_the_Field |archive-date=2024-11-09 |access-date=2025-11-10 |journal=IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine |date=2012 |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=98–100 |language=en |doi=10.1109/MRA.2012.2192811}}</ref> These feelings often result in instances of perceived lack of congruency, or when anthropomorphic attributions create expectations that robots don't meet; for example, when human-like appearance is paired with non-human behavior in a robot, or when robots have a human appearance but a synthetic voice.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Laakasuo |first1=Michael |last2=Palomäki |first2=Jussi |last3=Köbis |first3=Nils |date=2021-11-01 |title=Moral Uncanny Valley: A Robot's Appearance Moderates How its Decisions are Judged |journal=International Journal of Social Robotics |language=en |volume=13 |issue=7 |pages=1679–1688 |doi=10.1007/s12369-020-00738-6 |issn=1875-4805|doi-access=free |hdl=10138/336366 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mitchell |first1=Wade J. |last2=Szerszen |first2=Kevin A. |last3=Lu |first3=Amy Shirong |last4=Schermerhorn |first4=Paul W. |last5=Scheutz |first5=Matthias |last6=Macdorman |first6=Karl F. |date=2011 |title=A mismatch in the human realism of face and voice produces an uncanny valley |journal=i-Perception |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=10–12 |doi=10.1068/i0415 |issn=2041-6695 |pmc=3485769 |pmid=23145223}}</ref> Research has shown that repeated interactions with a robot can decrease these feelings of strangeness.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zlotowski |first1=Jakub Aleksander |last2=Sumioka |first2=Hidenobu |last3=Nishio |first3=Shuichi |last4=Glas |first4=Dylan F. |last5=Bartneck |first5=Christoph |last6=Ishiguro |first6=Hiroshi |date=2015-06-30 |title=Persistence of the uncanny valley: the influence of repeated interactions and a robot's attitude on its perception |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=6 |page=883 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00883 |pmid=26175702 |pmc=4484984 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078}}</ref>

==== Interactive behavior ====
Robots' nonverbal social behavior can influence anthropomorphizing. In general, highly interactive robots are more likely to be subject of attribution of mental states and competence, with friendly and polite behavior resulting in increased perceived trustworthiness and satisfaction.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Horstmann |first1=Aike C. |last2=Krämer |first2=Nicole C. |date=2020-08-21 |title=Expectations vs. actual behavior of a social robot: An experimental investigation of the effects of a social robot's interaction skill level and its expected future role on people's evaluations |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=15 |issue=8 |article-number=e0238133 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0238133 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=7446840 |pmid=32822438 |bibcode=2020PLoSO..1538133H }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Shikhar |last2=Itzhak |first2=Eliran |last3=Edan |first3=Yael |last4=Nimrod |first4=Galit |last5=Sarne-Fleischmann |first5=Vardit |last6=Tractinsky |first6=Noam |date=2022-10-01 |title=Politeness in Human–Robot Interaction: A Multi-Experiment Study with Non-Humanoid Robots |journal=International Journal of Social Robotics |language=en |volume=14 |issue=8 |pages=1805–1820 |doi=10.1007/s12369-022-00911-z |issn=1875-4805 |pmc=9387416 |pmid=35996386}}</ref> Within an interaction, unpredictable behavior can sometimes trigger increased anthropomorphization compared to clearly recognizable patterns of behavior.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Waytz |first1=Adam |last2=Morewedge |first2=Carey K. |last3=Epley |first3=Nicholas |last4=Monteleone |first4=George |last5=Gao |first5=Jia-Hong |last6=Cacioppo |first6=John T. |date=September 2010 |title=Making sense by making sentient: effectance motivation increases anthropomorphism |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |volume=99 |issue=3 |pages=410–435 |doi=10.1037/a0020240 |issn=1939-1315 |pmid=20649365}}</ref> At the same time, adherence to certain pragmatic expectations in interactions by replicating human details such as timing and turn-taking can also result in anthropomorphism.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Minato |first1=Takashi |last2=Sakai |first2=Kurima |last3=Uchida |first3=Takahisa |last4=Ishiguro |first4=Hiroshi |date=2022-10-11 |title=A study of interactive robot architecture through the practical implementation of conversational android |journal=Frontiers in Robotics and AI |language=English |volume=9 |article-number=905030 |doi=10.3389/frobt.2022.905030 |pmid=36304795 |pmc=9592984 |doi-access=free |issn=2296-9144}}</ref>

==== Movements ====
People tend to attribute more mental states to robots that perform gestures compared to those that are stationary; this effect is enhanced for robots that have multiple degrees of freedom in movement (such as being able to move on multiple different axes rather than on a single axis, such as up and down).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Salem |first1=Maha |last2=Eyssel |first2=Friederike |last3=Rohlfing |first3=Katharina |last4=Kopp |first4=Stefan |last5=Joublin |first5=Frank |date=2013-08-01 |title=To Err is Human(-like): Effects of Robot Gesture on Perceived Anthropomorphism and Likability |journal=International Journal of Social Robotics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=313–323 |doi=10.1007/s12369-013-0196-9 |issn=1875-4805}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kumazaki |first1=Hirokazu |last2=Muramatsu |first2=Taro |last3=Yoshikawa |first3=Yuichiro |last4=Matsumoto |first4=Yoshio |last5=Ishiguro |first5=Hiroshi |last6=Kikuchi |first6=Mitsuru |last7=Sumiyoshi |first7=Tomiki |last8=Mimura |first8=Masaru |date=2020 |title=Optimal robot for intervention for individuals with autism spectrum disorders |journal=Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences |language=en |volume=74 |issue=11 |pages=581–586 |doi=10.1111/pcn.13132 |issn=1440-1819 |pmc=7692924 |pmid=32827328}}</ref> Regardless of a robot's appearance, movement patterns that are more human-like are associated with greater anthropomorphism, as well as humans' increased feelings of pleasantness in an interaction.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kuz |first1=Sinem |last2=Mayer |first2=Marcel Ph. |last3=Müller |first3=Simon |last4=Schlick |first4=Christopher M. |chapter=Using Anthropomorphism to Improve the Human-Machine Interaction in Industrial Environments (Part I) |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2013 |volume=8026 |editor-last=Duffy |editor-first=Vincent G. |title=Digital Human Modeling and Applications in Health, Safety, Ergonomics, and Risk Management. Human Body Modeling and Ergonomics |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-39182-8_9 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=76–85 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-39182-8_9 |isbn=978-3-642-39182-8}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Castro-González |first1=Álvaro |last2=Admoni |first2=Henny |last3=Scassellati |first3=Brian |date=2016-06-01 |title=Effects of form and motion on judgments of social robots׳ animacy, likability, trustworthiness and unpleasantness |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S107158191600032X |journal=International Journal of Human-Computer Studies |volume=90 |pages=27–38 |doi=10.1016/j.ijhcs.2016.02.004 |hdl=10016/35083 |issn=1071-5819|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Linguistic factors ===
Given that the vast majority of public interactions with AI are through chatbots, these have been the primary focus of a great deal of research on AI anthropomorphism. A summary of a taxonomy of anthropomorphic features in linguistic AI systems in the literature follows:<ref name=":7">{{Citation |last1=Abercrombie |first1=Gavin |title=Mirages: On Anthropomorphism in Dialogue Systems |date=2023-10-23 |arxiv=2305.09800 |last2=Curry |first2=Amanda Cercas |last3=Dinkar |first3=Tanvi |last4=Rieser |first4=Verena |last5=Talat |first5=Zeerak}}</ref>

==== Voice ====
The outfitting of AI systems with auditory voices can be a significant factor in the anthropomorphism of linguistic agents. Research has shown that humans infer physical attributes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krauss |first1=Robert M |last2=Freyberg |first2=Robin |last3=Morsella |first3=Ezequiel |date=2002-11-01 |title=Inferring speakers' physical attributes from their voices |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022103102005103 |journal=Journal of Experimental Social Psychology |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=618–625 |doi=10.1016/S0022-1031(02)00510-3 |issn=0022-1031|url-access=subscription }}</ref> personality traits,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stern |first1=Julia |last2=Schild |first2=Christoph |last3=Jones |first3=Benedict C. |last4=DeBruine |first4=Lisa M. |last5=Hahn |first5=Amanda |last6=Puts |first6=David A. |last7=Zettler |first7=Ingo |last8=Kordsmeyer |first8=Tobias L. |last9=Feinberg |first9=David |last10=Zamfir |first10=Dan |last11=Penke |first11=Lars |last12=Arslan |first12=Ruben C. |date=2021-06-01 |title=Do voices carry valid information about a speaker's personality? |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092656621000295 |journal=Journal of Research in Personality |volume=92 |article-number=104092 |doi=10.1016/j.jrp.2021.104092 |issn=0092-6566|url-access=subscription |hdl=21.11116/0000-0005-BBF6-3 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> stereotypical traits,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shiramizu |first1=Victor Kenji M. |last2=Lee |first2=Anthony J. |last3=Altenburg |first3=Daria |last4=Feinberg |first4=David R. |last5=Jones |first5=Benedict C. |date=2022-12-28 |title=The role of valence, dominance, and pitch in perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agents' voices |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=22479 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-27124-8  |doi-access=free|pmid=36577918 |bibcode=2022NatSR..1222479S |issn=2045-2322|pmc=9797498 }}</ref> and emotion<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nass |first1=Clifford |url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262640657/wired-for-speech/ |title=Wired for Speech: How Voice Activates and Advances the Human-Computer Relationship |last2=Brave |first2=Scott |date=2007-02-23 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-64065-7 |location=Cambridge, MA, USA |language=en}}</ref> based on voice alone. Various changes in tone can influence the kind of personality users attribute to a voice, such as manipulations to breathiness, echoes, creakiness, reverberations, etc.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Sarah |last2=Moore |first2=Roger K. |date=2017 |title=Robot, Alien and Cartoon Voices: Implications for Speech-Enabled Systems | journal = 1st Int. Workshop on Vocal Interactivity In-and-between Humans, Animals and Robots (Pp. 40-44). |s2cid=231626780 }}</ref> The integration of disfluencies into speech (such as self-interruptions, repetitions, or hesitations like "um" or "uh") have been shown to effectively mimic the naturalness of human responses.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lieu |first=Johnny |date=2018-05-11 |title=Google's human-like AI assistant will disclose itself as a robot |url=https://mashable.com/article/google-duplex-disclosures-robot |access-date=2025-10-25 |website=Mashable |language=en}}</ref> And the implementation of accents has been used to imitate the local standard to boost societal acceptability and prestige, though it has been suggested that this can be used to exploit people's tendencies to trust in-group members.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Torre |first1=Ilaria |last2=Maguer |first2=Sébastien Le |chapter=Should robots have accents? |date=August 2020 |title=2020 29th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN) |chapter-url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9223599 |pages=208–214 |doi=10.1109/RO-MAN47096.2020.9223599 |isbn=978-1-7281-6075-7 |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:kth:diva-283665 }}</ref>

==== Content ====
AI dialogue systems often produce a variety of responses that run contrary to what might be expected of an inanimate system. For example, in response to direct questions about its nature (e.g. "Are you human or machine?"), some AIs fail to respond correctly,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gros |first1=David |last2=Li |first2=Yu |last3=Yu |first3=Zhou |chapter=The R-U-A-Robot Dataset: Helping Avoid Chatbot Deception by Detecting User Questions About Human or Non-Human Identity |date=August 2021 |editor-last=Zong |editor-first=Chengqing |editor2-last=Xia |editor2-first=Fei |editor3-last=Li |editor3-first=Wenjie |editor4-last=Navigli |editor4-first=Roberto |title=Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers) |chapter-url=https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.544/ |location=Online |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=6999–7013 |doi=10.18653/v1/2021.acl-long.544}}</ref> and they also sometimes make claims of engaging in uniquely human abilities such as having family relationships, consuming food, and crying.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Abercrombie |first1=Gavin |last2=Cercas Curry |first2=Amanda |last3=Pandya |first3=Mugdha |last4=Rieser |first4=Verena |date=August 2021 |editor-last=Costa-jussa |editor-first=Marta |editor2-last=Gonen |editor2-first=Hila |editor3-last=Hardmeier |editor3-first=Christian |editor4-last=Webster |editor4-first=Kellie |title=Alexa, Google, Siri: What are Your Pronouns? Gender and Anthropomorphism in the Design and Perception of Conversational Assistants |url=https://aclanthology.org/2021.gebnlp-1.4/ |journal=Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Gender Bias in Natural Language Processing |location=Online |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=24–33 |doi=10.18653/v1/2021.gebnlp-1.4|arxiv=2106.02578 }}</ref> AIs often output language that suggests they hold opinions, morals, or sentience.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=CIAIISC>{{cite arXiv |last1=Butlin |first1=Patrick |title=Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness |date=2023-08-22 |eprint=2308.08708 |last2=Long |first2=Robert |last3=Elmoznino |first3=Eric |last4=Bengio |first4=Yoshua |last5=Birch |first5=Jonathan |last6=Constant |first6=Axel |last7=Deane |first7=George |last8=Fleming |first8=Stephen M. |last9=Frith |first9=Chris |class=cs.AI }}</ref> Many AIs demonstrate agency and responsibility (such as by apologizing or otherwise acknowledging blame for mistakes), and they create the appearance of the human phenomenon of taboos by commonly avoiding contentious topics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mirnig |first1=Nicole |last2=Stollnberger |first2=Gerald |last3=Miksch |first3=Markus |last4=Stadler |first4=Susanne |last5=Giuliani |first5=Manuel |last6=Tscheligi |first6=Manfred |date=2017-05-31 |title=To Err Is Robot: How Humans Assess and Act toward an Erroneous Social Robot |journal=Frontiers in Robotics and AI |language=English |volume=4 |article-number=21 |doi=10.3389/frobt.2017.00021 |doi-access=free |issn=2296-9144}}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Glaese |first1=Amelia |title=Improving alignment of dialogue agents via targeted human judgements |date=2022-09-28 |eprint=2209.14375 |last2=McAleese |first2=Nat |last3=Trębacz |first3=Maja |last4=Aslanides |first4=John |last5=Firoiu |first5=Vlad |last6=Ewalds |first6=Timo |last7=Rauh |first7=Maribeth |last8=Weidinger |first8=Laura |last9=Chadwick |first9=Martin |class=cs.LG }}</ref> AIs which appear to produce empathy are increasingly anthropomorphic, though some research has shown that they are prone to producing inappropriate emotional amplification.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Ling.Yu |last2=Zhang |first2=Zhengkun |last3=Wang |first3=Jun |last4=Wang |first4=Hongbin |last5=Wu |first5=Haiying |last6=Yang |first6=Zhenglu |date=May 2022 |editor-last=Muresan |editor-first=Smaranda |editor2-last=Nakov |editor2-first=Preslav |editor3-last=Villavicencio |editor3-first=Aline |title=Multi-Party Empathetic Dialogue Generation: A New Task for Dialog Systems |url=https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.24/ |journal=Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) |location=Dublin, Ireland |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=298–307 |doi=10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.24|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Curry |first1=Alba |last2=Cercas Curry |first2=Amanda |date=July 2023 |editor-last=Rogers |editor-first=Anna |editor2-last=Boyd-Graber |editor2-first=Jordan |editor3-last=Okazaki |editor3-first=Naoaki |title=Computer says "No": The Case Against Empathetic Conversational AI |url=https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.515/ |journal=Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023 |location=Toronto, Canada |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=8123–8130 |doi=10.18653/v1/2023.findings-acl.515|arxiv=2212.10983 }}</ref> The use of first-person pronouns also contribute to anthropomorphic perceptions, as various studies have demonstrated that self-attribution is a critical part of the human condition and is read as a sign of consciousness.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Noonan |first=H. W. |date=2010-01-01 |title=The thinking animal problem and personal pronoun revisionism |url=https://academic.oup.com/analysis/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/analys/anp137 |journal=Analysis |language=en |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=93–98 |doi=10.1093/analys/anp137 |issn=0003-2638}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Olson |first=Eric T. |date=2002 |title=Thinking Animals and the Reference of 'I' |journal=Philosophical Topics |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=189–207 |doi=10.5840/philtopics20023016 |jstor=43154385 |issn=0276-2080}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-02-28 |title=On Human Nature {{!}} Princeton University Press |url=https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691168753/on-human-nature |access-date=2025-10-25 |website=press.princeton.edu |language=en}}</ref> AIs often appear to demonstrate self-awareness, referencing their own mechanistic processes with anthropomorphically loaded terms such as 'know', 'think', 'train', 'learn', 'understand', 'hallucinate' and 'intelligence'.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://zenodo.org/records/7524493 |title=Unhype Artificial 'Intelligence'! A proposal to replace the deceiving terminology of AI. |last=Hunger |first=Francis |date=2023-04-12 }}</ref><ref name=ShanahanM /><ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last1=Salles |first1=Arleen |last2=Evers |first2=Kathinka |last3=Farisco |first3=Michele |date=2020-04-02 |title=Anthropomorphism in AI |journal=AJOB Neuroscience |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=88–95 |doi=10.1080/21507740.2020.1740350 |issn=2150-7740 |pmid=32228388}}</ref>

==== Register and style ====
AI systems can appear more human through the use of phatic expressions, which are speech that humans use to facilitate social relations but that do not convey any information (such as [[small talk]]).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Leong |first1=Brenda |last2=Selinger |first2=Evan |chapter=Robot Eyes Wide Shut: Understanding Dishonest Anthropomorphism |date=2019-01-29 |title=Proceedings of the Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287591 |series=FAT* '19 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=299–308 |doi=10.1145/3287560.3287591 |isbn=978-1-4503-6125-5}}</ref> AI expressions of uncertainty, which are often implemented for the purpose of preventing the user from taking all outputs as factual, may boost anthropomorphic signals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=J. |first1=Mielke, Sabrina |last2=Arthur |first2=Szlam |last3=Emily |first3=Dinan |last4=Y-Lan |first4=Boureau |date=2022-12-23 |title=Reducing Conversational Agents' Overconfidence Through Linguistic Calibration |journal=Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics |language=en |volume=10 |pages=857–872 |doi=10.1162/tacl_a_00494 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2012.14983 }}</ref> Additionally, AIs are often designed to emulate character-based personas, which can overall have very strong anthropomorphic effects.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barron |first=Jesse |date=2025-10-24 |title=After Teen Suicide, Character.AI Lawsuit Raises Questions Over Free Speech Protections |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/24/magazine/character-ai-chatbot-lawsuit-teen-suicide-free-speech.html |access-date=2025-10-26 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==== Roles ====
AIs are also sometimes trained to play into roles that enhance anthropomorphic perceptions. For example, the majority of dialogue-based systems are designed to be in service of people in subservient roles; this has led to instances of users verbally abusing the systems, sometimes targeting them with gender-based slurs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lingel |first1=Jessa |last2=Crawford |first2=Kate |date=2020-05-15 |title=Alexa, Tell Me about Your Mother": The History of the Secretary and the End of Secrecy |url=https://catalystjournal.org/index.php/catalyst/article/view/29949 |journal=Catalyst: Feminism, Theory, Technoscience |language=en |volume=6 |issue=1 |doi=10.28968/cftt.v6i1.29949 |issn=2380-3312|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cercas Curry |first1=Amanda |last2=Abercrombie |first2=Gavin |last3=Rieser |first3=Verena |chapter=ConvAbuse: Data, Analysis, and Benchmarks for Nuanced Detection in Conversational AI |date=November 2021 |editor-last=Moens |editor-first=Marie-Francine |editor2-last=Huang |editor2-first=Xuanjing |editor3-last=Specia |editor3-first=Lucia |editor4-last=Yih |editor4-first=Scott Wen-tau |title=Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing |chapter-url=https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.587/ |location=Online and Punta Cana, Dominican Republic |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=7388–7403 |doi=10.18653/v1/2021.emnlp-main.587}}</ref> AI systems have been shown to sometimes respond even more subserviently to the abuse, perpetuating the behavior.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cercas Curry |first1=Amanda |last2=Rieser |first2=Verena |date=June 2018 |editor-last=Alfano |editor-first=Mark |editor2-last=Hovy |editor2-first=Dirk |editor3-last=Mitchell |editor3-first=Margaret |editor4-last=Strube |editor4-first=Michael |title=#MeToo Alexa: How Conversational Systems Respond to Sexual Harassment |url=https://aclanthology.org/W18-0802/ |journal=Proceedings of the Second ACL Workshop on Ethics in Natural Language Processing |location=New Orleans, Louisiana, USA |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=7–14 |doi=10.18653/v1/W18-0802}}</ref> AIs also often present as having a high degree of expertise; humans tend to infer higher credibility of outputs in these cases, as they would when presented with information from an expert human.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dinan |first1=Emily |last2=Abercrombie |first2=Gavin |last3=Bergman |first3=A. |last4=Spruit |first4=Shannon |last5=Hovy |first5=Dirk |last6=Boureau |first6=Y-Lan |last7=Rieser |first7=Verena |date=May 2022 |editor-last=Muresan |editor-first=Smaranda |editor2-last=Nakov |editor2-first=Preslav |editor3-last=Villavicencio |editor3-first=Aline |title=SafetyKit: First Aid for Measuring Safety in Open-domain Conversational Systems |url=https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.284/ |journal=Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) |location=Dublin, Ireland |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |pages=4113–4133 |doi=10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.284|doi-access=free |hdl=11565/4053224 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Human factors ==
In addition to AI factors contributing to anthropomorphizing, there are various features surrounding the user (i.e., the human interacting with the AI) that also play a role. The process of anthropomorphizing is very natural for humans and is ubiquitous across many different contexts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fritz Heider: An Experimental Study of Apparent Behavior |url=https://www.all-about-psychology.com/fritz-heider.html |access-date=2025-10-28 |website=Psychology}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mota-Rojas |first1=Daniel |last2=Mariti |first2=Chiara |last3=Zdeinert |first3=Andrea |last4=Riggio |first4=Giacomo |last5=Mora-Medina |first5=Patricia |last6=Del Mar Reyes |first6=Alondra |last7=Gazzano |first7=Angelo |last8=Domínguez-Oliva |first8=Adriana |last9=Lezama-García |first9=Karina |last10=José-Pérez |first10=Nancy |last11=Hernández-Ávalos |first11=Ismael |date=2021-11-15 |title=Anthropomorphism and Its Adverse Effects on the Distress and Welfare of Companion Animals |journal=Animals |volume=11 |issue=11 |page=3263 |doi=10.3390/ani11113263 |doi-access=free |issn=2076-2615 |pmc=8614365 |pmid=34827996}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Epley |first1=Nicholas |last2=Waytz |first2=Adam |last3=Cacioppo |first3=John T. |date=October 2007 |title=On seeing human: a three-factor theory of anthropomorphism |journal=Psychological Review |volume=114 |issue=4 |pages=864–886 |doi=10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864 |issn=0033-295X |pmid=17907867}}</ref> Epley et al. argue for a model with three psychological determinants that govern human tendencies to anthropomorphize.<ref name=":8" /> The first of those factors is elicited agent knowledge - the accessibility and applicability of knowledge about humans and the self, or the degree to which humans make inferences about other entities based on their own experience of being human. Individuals who tend to do this will anthropomorphize more; this explains why children anthropomorphize more than adults,<ref name=":9" /> since they lack complex models of nonhumans and rely heavily on self-based reasoning. The second factor in the model is effectance motivation – the need for humans to predict and reduce uncertainty in the environment. Anthropomorphizing can help people make sense of unpredictable phenomena by explaining them through intentional or human-like causes. Subsequent research has confirmed that individuals who express a need for order/closure and discomfort toward ambiguity tend to anthropomorphize more, possibly resulting from resolution of cognitive dissonance – human-like AIs may be highly ambiguous stimuli, and individuals who dislike ambiguity may be highly motivated to resolve the ambiguity by treating the AIs as more human.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nicolas |first1=Spatola |last2=Agnieszka |first2=Wykowska |date=2021-09-01 |title=The personality of anthropomorphism: How the need for cognition and the need for closure define attitudes and anthropomorphic attributions toward robots |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563221001643 |journal=Computers in Human Behavior |volume=122 |article-number=106841 |doi=10.1016/j.chb.2021.106841 |issn=0747-5632|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Finally, the third factor in the model is sociality motivation - the human need for social connection. People who feel chronically lonely or isolated may be increasingly likely to project human qualities onto non-human entities to satisfy their social needs.<ref name=":8" />

Research has shown that, in general, anthropomorphic tendencies vary based on norms, experience, education, cognitive reasoning styles, and attachment.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roselli |first1=Cecilia |last2=Lapomarda |first2=Leonardo |last3=Datteri |first3=Edoardo |date=2025-05-01 |title=How culture modulates anthropomorphism in Human-Robot Interaction: A review |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001691825001842 |journal=Acta Psychologica |volume=255 |article-number=104871 |doi=10.1016/j.actpsy.2025.104871 |pmid=40088562 |issn=0001-6918|hdl=10281/545361 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Users who are highly agreeable, for example, tend to be more susceptible to anthropomorphizing, as do individuals who are high in extraversion.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bernotat |first1=Jasmin |last2=Eyssel |first2=Friederike |chapter=A robot at home — How affect, technology commitment, and personality traits influence user experience in an intelligent robotics apartment |date=August 2017 |title=2017 26th IEEE International Symposium on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN) |pages=641–646 |doi=10.1109/ROMAN.2017.8172370 |isbn=978-1-5386-3518-6 |url=https://pub.uni-bielefeld.de/record/2914078 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Salem |first1=Maha |last2=Lakatos |first2=Gabriella |last3=Amirabdollahian |first3=Farshid |last4=Dautenhahn |first4=Kerstin |chapter=Would You Trust a (Faulty) Robot?: Effects of Error, Task Type and Personality on Human-Robot Cooperation and Trust |date=2015-03-02 |title=Proceedings of the Tenth Annual ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2696454.2696497 |series=HRI '15 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=141–148 |doi=10.1145/2696454.2696497 |isbn=978-1-4503-2883-8}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Park |first1=Eunil |last2=Jin |first2=Dallae |last3=del Pobil |first3=Angel P. |date=2012-08-21 |title=The Law of Attraction in Human-Robot Interaction |journal=International Journal of Advanced Robotic Systems |language=EN |volume=9 |issue=2 |page=35 |doi=10.5772/50228 |issn=1729-8806|hdl=10234/61945 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Individuals with attachment anxiety have been shown to more often anthropomorphize AI.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bartz |first1=Jennifer A. |last2=Tchalova |first2=Kristina |last3=Fenerci |first3=Can |date=2016-12-01 |title=Reminders of Social Connection Can Attenuate Anthropomorphism: A Replication and Extension of Epley, Akalis, Waytz, and Cacioppo (2008) |journal=Psychological Science |language=EN |volume=27 |issue=12 |pages=1644–1650 |doi=10.1177/0956797616668510 |pmid=27777375 |issn=0956-7976}}</ref> Young children are very prone to anthropomorphic attributions, but this propensity tends to decrease as children develop.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van Straten |first1=Caroline L. |last2=Peter |first2=Jochen |last3=Kühne |first3=Rinaldo |date=2020-05-01 |title=Child–Robot Relationship Formation: A Narrative Review of Empirical Research |journal=International Journal of Social Robotics |language=en |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=325–344 |doi=10.1007/s12369-019-00569-0 |issn=1875-4805 |pmc=7235061 |pmid=32454901}}</ref> Anthropomorphizing also tends to decrease with increased education and experience with technology.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Heerink |first=Marcel |chapter=Exploring the influence of age, gender, education and computer experience on robot acceptance by older adults |date=2011-03-06 |title=Proceedings of the 6th international conference on Human-robot interaction |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1957656.1957704 |series=HRI '11 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=147–148 |doi=10.1145/1957656.1957704 |isbn=978-1-4503-0561-7 |url=https://surfsharekit.nl/public/5555728b-4cb6-4f34-b5d2-b75e023074ea }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Niculescu |first1=Andreea |last2=van Dijk |first2=Betsy |last3=Nijholt |first3=Anton |last4=Li |first4=Haizhou |last5=See |first5=Swee Lan |date=2013-04-01 |title=Making Social Robots More Attractive: The Effects of Voice Pitch, Humor and Empathy |journal=International Journal of Social Robotics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=171–191 |doi=10.1007/s12369-012-0171-x |issn=1875-4805 |url=https://research.utwente.nl/en/publications/c616a396-411b-4a88-b49a-e4684eb24a97 }}</ref>

Additionally, some effects have been shown in research to be dependent on culture. For example, a negative correlation was found between loneliness and anthropomorphizing in Chinese individuals, compared to the positive link found in Western cultures.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Dang |first1=Jianning |last2=Liu |first2=Li |date=2023-04-01 |title=Do lonely people seek robot companionship? A comparative examination of the Loneliness–Robot anthropomorphism link in the United States and China |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563222004575 |journal=Computers in Human Behavior |volume=141 |article-number=107637 |doi=10.1016/j.chb.2022.107637 |issn=0747-5632|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Eyssel |first1=Friederike |last2=Reich |first2=Natalia |date=2013-03-03 |chapter=Loneliness makes the heart grow fonder (of robots): on the effects of loneliness on psychological anthropomorphism |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/2447556.2447597 |title=Proceedings of the 8th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-robot Interaction |location=Tokyo, Japan |publisher=IEEE Press |pages=121–122 |isbn=978-1-4673-3055-8}}</ref> This has been interpreted as possibly a result of differing drives for anthropomorphizing - people from Western cultures may anthropomorphize primarily as a means to counteract loneliness from a failure to cope with their social world, while people from East Asian cultures may already view nonhuman agents as part of their social world and anthropomorphize as a means of social exploration.<ref name=":10" /> Research has also shown that people tend to attribute more mental abilities and report more psychological closeness to robots that are presented as having the same cultural background as them.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eyssel |first1=Friederike |last2=Kuchenbrandt |first2=Dieta |date=2012 |title=Social categorization of social robots: Anthropomorphism as a function of robot group membership |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.2044-8309.2011.02082.x |journal=British Journal of Social Psychology |language=en |volume=51 |issue=4 |pages=724–731 |doi=10.1111/j.2044-8309.2011.02082.x |pmid=22103234 |issn=2044-8309|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Societal implications ==

=== Benefits and dangers ===
Some benefits to the anthropomorphism of AIs have been cited. For conversational agents, a human-like interactive interface and writing style has been demonstrated to have the ability to make dense sets of information more accessible and understandable in a variety of contexts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Dandan |last2=Zhang |first2=Shiqing |date=2024-09-20 |title=Large language models in medical and healthcare fields: applications, advances, }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hutchinson |first1=Maeve |title=Foundation model assisted visual analytics: Opportunities and Challenges |date=2025 |arxiv=2409.02691 |last2=Jianu |first2=Radu capable of role play as coaches or tutors, fine-tuning communication style and difficulty to individual comprehension levels effectively.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Zha |first1=Siyu |title=Mentigo: An |last2=Mollick |first2=Lilach |date=2023 |title=Assigning AI: Seven Approaches for Students, with Prompts |ssrn=4475995}}</ref> Role play agents can also be useful for entertainment or leisure On the other hand, anthropomorphized AI presents many novel dangers. Anthropomorphized AI algorithms are granted an implicit degree of agency that can have serious ethical implications when those systems are deployed in high-risk domains, like finance or clinical medicine.<ref name=":17">{{Cite SSRN |last1=Manuele |first1=Reani |last2=Xiangyang |first2=He |last3=Yunzhong |first3=Luo |last4=Zhida |first4=Sun |title=Fundamental Over-Attribution Error: |issn=0040-1625}}</ref> This can make users vulnerable to manipulation or exploitation; for example, anthropomorphized AIs can be more effective in convincing users to provide personal information or data, creating concerns for privacy.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Zhang |first1=Shuning |title="Ghost of the past": identifying and resolving privacy leakage from LLM's memory through proactive user interaction |date=2024-10-19 |eprint=2410.14931 |last2=Ye |first2=Lyumanshan |last3=Yi |first3=Xin |last4=Tang |first4=Jingyu |last5=Shui |first5=Bo |last6=Xing |first6=Haobin |last7=Liu |first7=Pengfei |last8=Li |first8=Hewu |class=cs.HC }}</ref> Humans who develop a significant level of trust in an AI assistant may rely excessively on the AI's advice or even defer important decisions entirely.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Akbulut |first1=Canfer |last2=Weidinger |first2=Laura |last3=Manzini |first3=Arianna |last4=Gabriel |first4=Iason |last5=Rieser |first5=Verena |date=2024-10-16 |title=All Too Human? Mapping and Mitigating the Risk from Anthropomorphic AI |url=https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AIES/article/view/31613 |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI/Acm Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=13–26 |doi=10.1609/aies.v7i1.31613 |issn=3065-8365|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Advanced LLMs are capable of using their human-like qualities to generate deceptive text, and research has found that they may be most persuasive when allowed to fabricate information and engage in deception.<ref name=":2" /> Some researchers suggest LLMs naturally have a particular aptitude for producing deceptive arguments, given that they are free from moral or ethical constraints that may inhibit human actors.<ref name=":3" /> Additionally, humans risk significant distress in establishing emotional dependence on AIs. Users may find that their expectations are violated, as AIs which may have seemed at first to play a role of a companion or romantic partner can exhibit unfeeling or unpredictable outputs, leading to feelings of profound betrayal or disappointment.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-03-30 |title=They fell in love with AI bots. A software update broke their hearts. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/03/30/replika-ai-chatbot-update/ |access-date=2025-11-03 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Users may also develop a false sense of responsibility for AI systems, suffering guilt if they perceive themselves to fail to meet the AI's needs at the expense of the user's own well-being.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Laestadius |first1=Linnea |last2=Bishop |first2=Andrea |last3=Gonzalez |first3=Michael |last4=Illenčík |first4=Diana |last5=Campos-Castillo |first5=Celeste |date=2024-10-01 |title=Too human and not human enough: A grounded theory analysis of mental health harms from emotional dependence on the social chatbot Replika |journal=New Media & Society |language=EN |volume=26 |issue=10 |pages=5923–5941 |doi=10.1177/14614448221142007 |issn=1461-4448}}</ref> Finally, anthropomorphizing AI can lead to exaggerations of its capabilities, potentially feeding into misinformation and exaggerated hopes and fears around AI.<ref name=":13" />

In many of today's practical contexts, it is not completely clear whether anthropomorphized AI produces positive or negative effects. For example, AI companions, which leverage anthropomorphic qualities of LLMs to give a convincing sense to users of human-likeness, have been credited with alleviating loneliness and suicidal ideation;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maples |first1=Bethanie |last2=Cerit |first2=Merve |last3=Vishwanath |first3=Aditya |last4=Pea |first4=Roy |date=2024-01-22 |title=Loneliness and suicide mitigation for students using GPT3-enabled chatbots |journal=npj Mental Health Research |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=4 |doi=10.1038/s44184-023-00047-6  |doi-access=free|pmid=38609517 |pmc=10955814 |issn=2731-4251}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Weijers |first1=Dan |last2=Munn |first2=Nick |date=2024-05-08 |title=AI companions can relieve loneliness – but here are 4 red flags to watch for in your chatbot 'friend' |url=http://theconversation.com/ai-companions-can-relieve-loneliness-but-here-are-4-red-flags-to-watch-for-in-your-chatbot-friend-227338 |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref> however, some analysis suggests that loneliness reduction could be short-lived,<ref name=":1" /> and AI companions have also been directly implicated in cases of suicide and self-harm.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-12-06 |title=AI friendships claim to cure loneliness. Some are ending in suicide. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2024/12/06/ai-companion-chai-research-character-ai/ |access-date=2025-10-23 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Allyn |first=Bobby |date=2024-12-10 |title=Lawsuit: A chatbot hinted a kid should kill his parents over screen time limits |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/12/10/nx-s1-5222574/kids-character-ai-lawsuit |access-date=2025-10-23 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref> Additionally, persuasive writing from LLMs have been shown to dissuade users from beliefs in conspiracy theories and to motivate users to donate to charitable causes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Costello |first1=Thomas H. |last2=Pennycook |first2=Gordon |last3=Rand |first3=David G. |date=2024-09-13 |title=Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adq1814 |journal=Science |volume=385 |issue=6714 |article-number=eadq1814 |doi=10.1126/science.adq1814 |pmid=39264999 |bibcode=2024Sci...385q1814C |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Sanghyub John |last2=Paas |first2=Leo |last3=Ahn |first3=Ho Seok |date=2024-09-01 |title=The power of specific emotion analysis in predicting donations: A comparative empirical study between sentiment and specific emotion analysis in social media |journal=International Journal of Market Research |language=EN |volume=66 |issue=5 |pages=610–630 |doi=10.1177/14707853241261248 |issn=1470-7853|doi-access=free }}</ref> but it has also been associated with deception and various harmful outcomes.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Park |first1=Peter S. |title=AI Deception: A Survey of Examples, Risks, and Potential Solutions |date=2023-08-28 |eprint=2308.14752 |last2=Goldstein |first2=Simon |last3=O'Gara |first3=Aidan |last4=Chen |first4=Michael |last5=Hendrycks |first5=Dan |class=cs.CY }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Measuring the Persuasiveness of Language Models |url=https://www.anthropic.com/research/measuring-model-persuasiveness |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=www.anthropic.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shanahan |first1=Murray |last2=McDonell |first2=Kyle |last3=Reynolds |first3=Laria |date=November 2023 |title=Role play with large language models |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06647-8 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=623 |issue=7987 |pages=493–498 |doi=10.1038/s41586-023-06647-8 |pmid=37938776 |arxiv=2305.16367 |bibcode=2023Natur.623..493S |issn=1476-4687}}</ref> Researchers today cite a need for further dedicated research on the effects of anthropomorphized AIs to best inform decisions about implementation and spread of AI agents.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Peter |first1=Sandra |last2=Riemer |first2=Kai |last3=West |first3=Jevin D. |date=2025-06-03 |title=The benefits and dangers of anthropomorphic conversational agents |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=122 |issue=22 |article-number=e2415898122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2415898122 |doi-access=free |pmc=12146756 |pmid=40378006 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12215898P }}</ref>

Anticipation of the ubiquity of anthropomorphic AI systems has led to concern over potential harms that may not be entirely realized today. In particular, some researchers foresee that the delineation between what is actually human and what is merely human-like may become less clear as the gap between human and AI capabilities grows smaller and smaller.<ref name=":5" /> This, some argue, may adversely affect human collective self-determination, as non-human entities gradually begin to shape our core value systems and influence society.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Milossi |first1=Maria |last2=Alexandropoulou-Egyptiadou |first2=Eugenia |last3=Psannis |first3=Konstantinos E. |date=2021 |title=AI Ethics: Algorithmic Determinism or Self-Determination? The GPDR Approach |journal=IEEE Access |volume=9 |pages=58455–58466 |doi=10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3072782 |bibcode=2021IEEEA...958455M |issn=2169-3536|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Laitinen |first1=Arto |last2=Sahlgren |first2=Otto |date=2021-10-26 |title=AI Systems and Respect for Human Autonomy |journal=Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence |language=English |volume=4 |article-number=705164 |doi=10.3389/frai.2021.705164 |pmid=34765969 |pmc=8576577 |doi-access=free |issn=2624-8212}}</ref> It may also lead to the degradation of human social connections, as humans may come to prefer interacting with AI systems that are designed with user satisfaction as a priority; this can have a multitude of negative implications. For example, AI agents already display a significant degree of sycophancy, which means that an increasing role for AI agents in users' opinion space may result in increased polarization and a decrease in value placed in others' beliefs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Naddaf |first=Miryam |date=2025-10-24 |title=AI chatbots are sycophants — researchers say it's harming science |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-03390-0 |journal=Nature |volume=647 |issue=8088 |pages=13–14 |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-025-03390-0 |pmid=41136779 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Acclimatization to the conventions of human-AI interaction may undermine the value we place on human individuality and self-expression, or may lead to inappropriate expectations derived from AI interactions being placed on human interactions.<ref name=":5" /> In general, human social connectedness is known to play a critical role in individual and group well-being, and its replacement with AI interactions may result in mass dissatisfaction or lack of fulfillment.<ref>{{Cite web |last=CDC |date=2024-05-22 |title=Social Connection |url=https://www.cdc.gov/social-connectedness/about/index.html |access-date=2025-10-30 |website=Social Connection |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Turkle |first1=Sherry |date=2018-08-11 |title=Opinion {{!}} There Will Never Be an Age of Artificial Intimacy (Published 2018) |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/11/opinion/there-will-never-be-an-age-of-artificial-intimacy.html |access-date=2025-10-30 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Proposed directions ===

Given the demonstrated and projected effects of AI anthropomorphism, a variety of suggestions have been made intending to inform future development of AI. Much of this discourse is centered around curbing the most harmful effects of anthropomorphism. For example, some researchers have called for a moratorium on the use of language which deliberately invokes humanness; this applies both to how AI companies describe their products<ref>{{Cite web |title=Learning to reason with LLMs |url=https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/ |access-date=2025-11-03 |website=openai.com |language=en-US}}</ref> and the language output by the systems themselves. Particularly, it has been suggested that terms like "seeing", "thinking", and "reasoning" should be replaced by terms like "recognizing", "computing", and "inferring", and that first-person pronouns such as "I" and "my" should not be used by chatbots.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":7" /> Another idea is the implementation of a specific AI accent or dialect that would clearly indicate when language was generated artificially.<ref name=":6" /> However, given the commercial pressures to optimize AI agents for economic gain – which may involve exploiting anthropomorphic qualities – it may not be prudent to rely on the restraint of developers, meaning that increased regulation may be necessary to limit harms. As of now, there are no laws that directly address anthropomorphism in AI; potential avenues for regulation include requirements for transparency and built-in safeguard mechanisms.<ref name=":3" /> More generally, researchers cite a need for increased understanding of the kinds and degrees of anthropomorphic qualities possessed by AI systems. To that end, it has been proposed that new benchmarks and tests should be developed that measure anthropomorphic qualities in AI writing, inference, and interaction.<ref name=":3" />

== In popular culture ==
{{AI-generated|section=y|date=September 2026}}
Anthropomorphic portrayals of AI are common in film, literature, and other interactive media. These depictions often emphasize human-like qualities of AI in ways that shape public perceptions.

=== Film and television ===
There are a number of well-known portrayals in movies and TV of AI possessing human-like agency or personalities. In film, [[HAL 9000]] in ''[[2001: A Space Odyssey]]'' and Ava in ''[[Ex Machina (film)|Ex Machina]]'' are depicted with complex emotions and motives.<ref>''2001: A Space Odyssey''. Directed by Stanley Kubrick. Warner Home Video, 1999.</ref><ref>Garland, A. (2014). ''Ex Machina''. A24.</ref> Television portrayals include Data from ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]'' and [[KITT]] from ''[[Knight Rider]].''<ref>''Star Trek, The Next Generation. [United States] :Paramount Pictures, 1987-1994.''</ref><ref>''Knight Rider''. Created by Glen A. Larson, NBC, 1982–1986.</ref>

=== Literature ===
Anthropomorphic AI is also common in literature. [[Isaac Asimov]]'s robot characters, including [[R. Daneel Olivaw]], exhibit human reasoning and moral dilemmas, while [[Iain Banks]]'s "Minds" in ''[[Culture series|The Culture]]'' series are portrayed as having distinct personalities and social roles.<ref>Asimov, I. (1991). ''The caves of steel.'' Bantam.</ref><ref>Banks, I. (2024). ''The state of the art.'' First Orbit U.S. edition. Orbit.</ref>

=== Video games ===
Examples of anthropomorphized AI in video games include [[GLaDOS]] in ''[[Portal (video game)|Portal]]'', a witty and sinister guide for the player, and [[Cortana (Halo)|Cortana]] in the ''[[Halo (franchise)|Halo]]'' series, who forms emotional bonds with human protagonists.<ref>''Portal''. The Orange Box, Valve, 2007</ref><ref>''Halo: Combat Evolved''. Developed by Bungie, Microsoft Game Studios, 2001. Xbox.</ref>

=== Advertising and consumer technology ===
Marketing campaigns for digital assistants such as [[Amazon Alexa]], [[Google Assistant]], and [[Siri]] often portray the systems as personable or empathetic.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Monteverde |first1=Giulia |last2=Cammarota |first2=Antonella |last3=Serafini |first3=Ludovica |last4=Quadri |first4=Martina |date=2025-01-02 |title=Are we human or are we voice assistants?
