* {{Anchor|Spoon}}'''Spoon:''' For much of seasons 1, 2, and 3, Carmy often seems to "[[Stimming|stim]]" in the kitchen with an "emotional-support spoon" he carries around with him.<ref name="sc">{{Cite web |last=Daut |first=David |date=Fall 2024 |title=The Bear - Every Second Counts: A Conversation with Gary Malouf & Chris Dame |url=https://soc.org/project/the-bear/ |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Society of Camera Operators Magazine |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-11-19  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241119021943/https://soc.org/project/the-bear/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Camera operator Gary Malouf stated in an interview: "[Our job is] find those textures that the actors are so good at bringing. [In season one], Jeremy would just be waiting to go while they reset all the food, but he'd keep tapping that spoon like crazy—someone shoot that. We were constantly trying to find these little details that could help build the world around us without ever feeling like we were in anybody's way."<ref name="sc"/> While asking Tina about his mom in season 1, "he nervously drums a spoon between his thumb and forefinger."<ref name="McFarland-7fish">{{Cite web |last=McFarland |first=Melanie |date=June 29, 2023 |title=''The Bear'' hides crusts of meaning and trauma in an episode about the Feast of the Seven Fishes |url=https://www.salon.com/2023/06/29/the-bear-hides-crusts-of-meaning-and-trauma-in-an-episode-about-the-feast-of-the-seven-fishes/ |access-date=2026-09-19 |website=Salon.com |language=en-US}}</ref> After Sweeps and Tina put out the fire Carmy accidentally set in the kitchen in "[[Braciole (The Bear)|Braciole]]," he is refocused by Richie and then seems to be reflexively reaching for the spoon he usually keeps at the small of his back, but it's not there. In the season 3 premiere episode "[[Tomorrow (The Bear)|Tomorrow]]," the origin story of the spoon is told: once upon a time, mentor [[Andrea Terry|Chef Terry]] ([[Olivia Colman]]) ceded control of [[Sauce|saucing]] a dish, tacitly acknowledging Carmy as a worthy successor, at which time she quietly told him, "keep the spoon." In "Green," Carmy, in turn, passes the torch to Sydney, handing her his "emotional-support spoon" as a gesture of trust in anticipation of his forthcoming departure from day-to-day management of the Bear. Carmy's spoon is most likely a [[Gray Kunz]]-brand sauce spoon, which is "a workhorse of restaurant kitchens" and "beloved by professional chefs".<ref name="wirecutter-2024">{{Cite news |last=Aciman |first=Alexander |date=June 28, 2024 |title=''The Bear'' Is Back. Here's Every Wirecutter Pick We've Spotted in Carmy's Kitchen |url=https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/the-bear-season-2-return-carmys-kitchen-picks/ |access-date=2026-01-09 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="StJohn-2026" /> Eventually, other chefs in Carmy's kitchen begin "almost fetishizing this slightly oversized spoon...In [season 5], we actually see Sydney tuck it in the back of her apron, almost the way a gunfighter might hide a [[Colt revolver]]...at least one character uses the spoon to make a point in season 4. When Tina asks Carmy if he's seen his sister Natalie's newborn, and he responds, 'Which baby?' she waves the Gray Kunz at him" and gives him a few choice words.<ref name="StJohn-2026" /> One of Carmy's [[wikiquote:The Bear (TV series)#%22Replicants%22 %5B4.05%5D|most actionable "non-negotiables"]] is "never run out of [[Teaspoon|teaspoons]],"<ref name="Chaney-2024nonnego">{{Cite web |last=Chaney |first=Jen |date=June 28, 2024 |title=''The Bear''{{'s}} Non-Negotiables, Ranked by Negotiability |url=https://www.vulture.com/article/the-bear-season-3-non-negotiables-list.html |access-date=2026-09-20 |website=Vulture |language=en}}</ref> but there is a distinct spoon shortage in season 5. Carmy {{Linktext|double-dips}} with the same [[tasting spoon]] ''and'' licks his fingers while tasting Syd's cola-ribs sauce, which, for fancy-chef him, is insane. Ebra the fox investigates, eventually revealing Marcus the hyena as a spoon hoarder: "You are the son of a bitch...Now other people are short spoons."<ref name="Chaney-TOBOC2026">{{Cite web |last=Chaney |first=Jen |date=June 26, 2026 |title=''The Bear'' Season-Finale Recap: Let It Rip. And R.I.P. |url=https://www.vulture.com/article/the-bear-finale-recap-season-5-episode-8-the-original-beef-of-chicagoland.html |access-date=2026-09-19 |website=Vulture |language=en}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Civility
======================================================================

{{short description|Polite act or expression}}
{{for|the project page about orderly conduct on Wikipedia|Wikipedia:Civility}}
'''Civility''' may denote orderly behavior and [[politeness]]. Historically, civility also meant training in the [[humanities]].

==Definition==
Civility has been described as among the most valuable of the social virtues. In this context it has been described as the skill of discussing topics that are important to one with others who disagree with and do so without any serious falling out. An alternative meaning of the term Civility is to describe the some limits on acceptable behaviour. In this sense it can reflect a problematic society one in which rights such as equality or humanity are extended only to those who are deemed to be sufficiently civil. These are two extreme positions between which are range of different views and approaches to Civility have been argued. Civility is an idea that many philosophers especially after [[The Reformation]] when rival approaches to the seeking of salvation appeared to make disagreement difficult if civility was to be maintained.<ref>BBC (2025) [[In Our Time (radio series)|In Our Time]]: Civility https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m002f9f4</ref><ref>Bejan, Teresa M. (2017) Mere Civility: Disagreement and the Limits of Toleration (Harvard University Press)</ref><ref>Burke, Peter (1995) The Fortunes of the Courtier: The European Reception of Castiglione's Cortegiano (Polity Press)</ref><ref>Bybee, Keith J. (2016) How Civility Works (Stanford University Press)</ref><ref>Thomas, Keith (2018) In Pursuit of Civility: Manners and Civilization in Early Modern England (Yale University Press)</ref><ref>Withington, Phil (2010) Society in Early Modern England: The Vernacular Origins of Some Powerful Ideas (Polity)</ref>

Key early works on civility include:
* [[Baldassare Castiglione]]'s 1528 [[The Book of the Courtier]]
* [[Erasmus]]'s 1530 [[On Civility in Children]]

==Developmental model==
Adolf G. Gundersen and Suzanne Goodney Lea developed a civility model grounded in empirical data that "stresses the notion that civility is a sequence, not a single thing or set of things". The model conceives of civility as a continuum or scale consisting of increasingly demanding traits ranging from "indifference" to "commentary", "conversation", "co-exploration" and, from there, to "habituation". According to the authors, such a developmental model has several advantages, not least of which is that it allows civility to be viewed as something everyone can get better at.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gundersen|first1=Adolf G.|first2= Suzanne Goodney|last2=Lea |title=Let's Talk Politics: Restoring Civility through Exploratory Discussion |publisher=Interactivity Foundation |location=Parkersburg, W.Va. |date=March 14, 2013}}</ref>

==Empathy in civility==
Many civility experts say civility goes beyond good manners and listening attentively, but includes sharing our own beliefs and values with others through some type of engagement with the intent of sincere respect towards one another. This also requires a willingness and open mindedness to having our opinions and biases challenged by others who share different and perhaps unique [[Point of view (philosophy)|points of view]].<ref>{{cite web |title= Why Civility Matters |url= https://civilitymatters.org/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110627053949/http://civilitymatters.org/ |url-status= usurped |archive-date= June 27, 2011 |access-date= 2020-07-05 |date= 2020}}</ref>

Civility experts say that our ability to act with civility is connected with our ability to understand our own [[emotions]]. Understanding our feelings helps us to recognize how we are feeling in real-time and give us a greater ability to have [[empathy]] for others. Furthermore, discerning and recognizing our feelings can help us to evaluate the things that trigger us emotionally and therefore become more aware of how we will possibly react and feel in certain situations. By taking the time to understand our thoughts and emotions in these situations, this practice can lead to self-recognition and acceptance of how similar situations may affect others, including those that may share a unique perspective.<ref>{{cite web |title= Why The Key to Civility is Empathy |website=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/forbescoachescouncil/2018/02/08/why-the-key-to-civility-is-empathy/#2dc15a1172e8 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200705210846/https://www.forbes.com/sites/forbescoachescouncil/2018/02/08/why-the-key-to-civility-is-empathy/#2dc15a1172e8 |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 5, 2020 |access-date=2020-07-05 |date= 2018-02-08}}</ref>

Sharon Styles-Anderson established Emotional Civility Day, March 6. Emotional Civility, a concept developed by Anderson, helps the world recognize that there is a connection between the way people feel and the way they interact with others.

==Lack of civility==
{{Main|Incivility}}{{Update|part=section|date=September 2025}}
Incivility is the opposite of civility—a lack of civility. Verbal or physical attacks on others, [[cyber bullying]], [[rudeness]], [[religious intolerance]], [[discrimination]], and [[vandalism]] are some of the acts that are generally considered uncivil. Incivility is an issue on the global stage.<ref>{{cite web |title= Incivility in Political Discourse (The Coming Apogee of the Moonbat Hordes) |work= InDC Journal |url= http://www.indcjournal.com/archives/001136.php |access-date= 2006-11-25 |date= 2004-10-13 |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://archive.today/20130103133948/http://www.indcjournal.com/archives/001136.php |archive-date= 2013-01-03}}</ref> Social media and the web give people the ability to freely exchange ideas, but this has not come without consequences.

Politicians in the U.S. frequently say that they encounter a lack of civility in their workplace, and have disregarded it as unfortunate aspect of politics. But polls indicate that "going negative" can help candidates win elections. During the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential campaign]], candidate [[Donald Trump]] regularly called his rivals "stupid, incompetent, and losers," <ref>{{cite web |title= Bush Appeals for Civility in GOP Race |work=US News |url=https://www.usnews.com/news/blogs/ken-walshs-washington/2015/07/28/bush-appeals-for-civility-in-gop-race |access-date=2015-08-16 |date= 2015-07-28}}</ref> while his opponent [[Hillary Clinton]] referred to his voters as a "basket of deplorables."<ref>{{cite news |last=Montanaro |first=Domenico |title=Hillary Clinton's 'Basket Of Deplorables,' In Full Context Of This Ugly Campaign |url=https://www.npr.org/2016/09/10/493427601/hillary-clintons-basket-of-deplorables-in-full-context-of-this-ugly-campaign |work=NPR |date=September 10, 2016 |access-date=September 10, 2026}}</ref>

Recognizing that people harassing others online has become a problem and can have negative consequences for businesses, many companies stepped up to create more awareness and initiatives to help. [[Intel]] in collaboration with organizations such as the [[Born This Way Foundation]] and [[Vox Media]] initiated "Hack Harassment" aimed to increase awareness of online harassment and anti-harassment technologies.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hack Harassment |url=http://www.hackharassment.com/ |url-status=dead |access-date=2016-01-17 |date=2016-01-17 |archive-date=2016-01-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160113124144/http://www.hackharassment.com/}}</ref> {{As of|2016}} the Data & Society/CiPHR Measuring Cyberabuse poll indicated that nearly 70% of people between the ages of 15 and 29 are harassed or abused online.<ref>{{cite web |title= Hack Harassment Announces Formation of Advisory Board to Elevate the Dialogue Around Online Harassment |work=Intel Newsroom |url=https://newsroom.intel.com/news-releases/hack-harassment-announces-formation-advisory-board-elevate-dialogue-around-online-harassment/ |access-date=2021-03-24 |date= 2017-05-01}}</ref> Although there are tactics to block cyber-bullying, such as censorship and banning users from accessing a site, it does not correct the underlying issues on what causes it. 75% of technology professionals believe a universal code of online conduct would also help curb online harassment.<ref>{{cite web |title= Intel, Vox Media, Re/code and Lady Gaga's Born This Way Foundation to Hack Online Harassment |work=Intel Newsroom |url=https://newsroom.intel.com/news-releases/intel-vox-media-recode-and-lady-gagas-born-this-way-foundation-to-hack-online-harassment/ |access-date=2021-03-24 |date= 2016-01-07}}</ref>

On April 22, 2016, The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research at the [[University of Chicago]] released a report citing that 74 percent of Americans think manners and behavior have declined in the United States. In this study they discovered that people in most cases can agree with what is appropriate and [[inappropriateness|inappropriate]] behavior. They found that 8 out of 10 Americans find jokes made based on race, gender, or sexuality are considered inappropriate, but only a small number of people own up to making these types of jokes. The report suggests that nearly half of all Americans aged 18–29 find it acceptable to use their cell phones in a restaurant, while fewer than 22 percent of people over the age of 60 agree.<ref>{{cite web |title= Americans believe civility is on the decline |work= The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research at the University of Chicago |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/04/160422201040.htm |access-date=2016-05-24 |date= 2016-04-22}}</ref>

==Critiques of civility in politics==

Although calls for civility are made by politicians across political parties and ideologies, some scholars question whether political civility and resistance to incivility can lead to harmful consequences.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bejan |first1=Teresa |title=Mere Civility: Disagreement and the Limits of Toleration |date=2017 |publisher=Harvard University Press |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |isbn=9780674545496 |page=1 |jstor=j.ctv253f8fg |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv253f8fg |access-date=20 October 2025}}</ref> [[Alex Zamalin]] argues that criticism of uncivil political discourse can detract attention from the substance of peoples' views by centering discussion of the tone with which ideas are delivered rather than their content.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zamalin |first1=Alex |title=Against Civility: The Hidden Racism in Our Obsession with Civility |date=2021 |publisher=Beacon Press |location=Boston, Massachusetts |isbn=9780807026540 |pages=7–8}}</ref> Additionally, rhetorical critics Nina Lozano-Reich and Dana Cloud observe that dominant groups have historically used appeals for civility in politics to silence and marginalize historically oppressed groups. As an example, Lozano-Reich and Cloud point out that, in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, notions of "civilization" and "civility" were used to justify the exclusion of women from the public sphere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lozano-Reich |first1=Nina |last2=Cloud |first2=Dana |title=The Uncivil Tongue: Invitational Rhetoric and the Problem of Inequality |journal=Western Journal of Communication |date=2009 |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=223–224 |doi=10.1080/10570310902856105 |url= https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10570310902856105 |access-date=20 October 2025|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Jasbir Puar also notes that historically oppressed groups such as people of color and immigrants are more likely to be regarded as uncivil because of discriminatory ideas about these groups.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lê Espiritu |first1=Evyn |last2=Puar |first2=Jasbir |title=Civility, Academic Freedom, and the Project of Decolonization: A Conversation with Steven Salaita |journal=Qui Parle |date=2015 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=64–65 |doi=10.5250/quiparle.24.1.0063 |jstor=10.5250/quiparle.24.1.0063 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.5250/quiparle.24.1.0063 |access-date=20 October 2025}}</ref> These dynamics are further complicated by societal elites having greater power than marginalized groups in defining what counts as civil versus uncivil.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zamalin |first1=Alex |title=Against Civility: The Hidden Racism in Our Obsession with Civility |date=2021 |publisher=Beacon Press |location=Boston, Massachusetts |isbn=9780807026540 |pages=8}}</ref> Thus, as Lozano-Reich and Cloud argue, political equality among different social groups is likely required for both civil discourse and appeals for civil discourse to yield productive dialogue that does not marginalize members of historically oppressed groups.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lozano-Reich |first1=Nina |last2=Cloud |first2=Dana |title=The Uncivil Tongue: Invitational Rhetoric and the Problem of Inequality |journal=Western Journal of Communication |date=2009 |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=224–225 |doi=10.1080/10570310902856105 |url= https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10570310902856105 |access-date=20 October 2025|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Movements to foster civility==

===Worldwide===
In October 2019, the [[United Nations]] announced that the World Civility Index would be a part of their [[Sustainable Development Goals]] (SDGs).<ref name=softskills/> The new Sustainable Development Goals initiative serves as the updated global targets that were set forth initially in the [[Millennium Development Goals]] (MDGs) of 2000 to 2015. Under the Sustainable Development Goals initiatives, the United Nations identified seventeen core challenges that have an interconnected part in achieving a more sustainable future for all.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/sustainable-development-goals/ |title=About the Sustainable Development Goals |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=n.d. |access-date=July 6, 2020}}</ref> The World Civility Index is designed to be implemented as a tool for employers and organizations around the world to create a system of consistent measurements of soft skills that are related to civility.<ref name=softskills/> Other global organizations, such as the Worldwide Civility Council, also aim to centralize civility resources and tools, such as the Civility Scorecard and Masonic Family Civility Project, in order to help promote civility and assist various civility organizations around the world.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://civilitycouncil.org/ |title=Working to restore civility in society |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=n.d. |access-date=July 6, 2020}}</ref> One of the core ideas promoted by the United Nations' goal on achieving worldwide civility is having a universal system for measuring civility, because setting a standard of measurement helps to more accurately measure levels of civility.<ref name=softskills>{{cite web |url=https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/partnership/?p=32946 |title=World Civility Index – Improve Youth's Soft Skills, and Standardizing Measurement For It, For Decent Jobs |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=2019 |access-date=July 6, 2020}}</ref> Furthermore, having meaningful measurements will help in creating more effective and efficient training to assist people in acquiring the soft skills needed, such as civility, in the modern workplace and foreseeable future.<ref name=softskills />

In 2020, the Worldwide Civility Council launched the Certified Civil initiative to recognize the commitment to civil behavior and communication by individuals, organizations, and groups around the world, which also includes but is not limited to businesses, publications, websites, and social media sites.<ref>{{cite web|title=About Certified Civil|url=https://certifiedcivil.org/about/|website=Certified Civil|access-date=24 March 2021}}</ref> A Certified Civil designation can only be awarded based on a demonstrated ability to act and foster civility. At the core of the civility certification process are several commitments, including advocating for dignity and respect in all dealings, listening to create constructive dialogues, speaking in a manner that reflects respect, ensuring all public content is within bounds defined by the Certified Civil standards, displaying the Certified Civil logo, and maintaining good standing through continuous certification.<ref>{{cite web|title=Certified Civil – Because Respect is the Foundation of Productive Dialogue|url=https://certifiedcivil.org/|website=Certified Civil|access-date=24 March 2021}}</ref>

===In the United States===

====Opinion polls====
A 2010 Allegheny College poll found that nearly all Americans (95 percent) believe civility is important in politics.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Levine|first1=Peter|title=We Are the Ones We Have Been Waiting For: The Promise of Civic Renewal in America|date=2013|publisher=Oxford University Press|asin=B00F51ZXII|edition=Kindle, first}}</ref>

In a 2012 poll conducted by [[Weber Shandwick]], 65% of Americans reported an increase in incivility due to a weakened U.S. economy during the Great Recession. Almost 50% of those Americans indicated they have removed themselves from participating in politics because of fear of incivility or bullying. Of the 1000 people surveyed, a follow-up study revealed that 86% of those people reported being subjected to incivility.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Williams |first=Ray |date=July 15, 2012 |title=The Rise of Incivility and Bullying in America |url=https://www.psychologytoday.com/blog/wired-success/201207/the-rise-incivility-and-bullying-in-america |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020000000/https://www.psychologytoday.com/blog/wired-success/201207/the-rise-incivility-and-bullying-in-america |archive-date=2014-10-20 |access-date=August 7, 2015 |publisher=Psychology Today}} [https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/20141020121023-1011572-the-rise-of-incivility-and-bullying-in-america Alt URL]</ref> In this report, part of an annual follow-up research report in January 2016 sharing findings on attitudes and sentiment about civility, 95% of Americans believe that incivility is a very visible issue, while 74% recognized that civility in general had declined during the past few years. Over 90% of voters claimed that the presidential candidates' attitudes and civil behavior would play a significant role in their voting decision in the upcoming 2016 election.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Ray Williams |title=Nearly All Likely Voters Say Candidates' Civility Will Affect Their Vote; New Poll Finds 93% Say Behavior Will Matter |publisher=Weber Shandwick |date=January 28, 2016 |url=http://www.webershandwick.com/news/article/nearly-all-likely-voters-say-candidates-civility-will-affect-their-vote |url-status=dead |access-date=February 7, 2016 |archive-date=February 2, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202072055/http://www.webershandwick.com/news/article/nearly-all-likely-voters-say-candidates-civility-will-affect-their-vote}}</ref>

In poll conducted by [[Georgetown University]] in 2019, 88% of Americans polled expressed concern and frustration about uncivil and rude behavior of many politicians.<ref name="Georgetown Institute of Politics and Public Service">{{Cite web |author=Georgetown Institute of Politics and Public Service |title=NEW POLL: Voters Find Political Divisions So Bad, Believe U.S. Is Two-Thirds Of The Way To "Edge Of A Civil War" |publisher=Georgetown University |date=October 23, 2019 |url=https://politics.georgetown.edu/2019/10/23/new-poll-voters-find-political-divisions-so-bad-believe-u-s-is-two-thirds-of-the-way-to-edge-of-a-civil-war/ |access-date=March 23, 2021}}</ref> 87% said they are {{clarify|text="|reason=where does this quote end?|date=July 2023}}tired of leaders compromising their values and ideals, while 80% of those same Americans want both "compromise and common ground" as well as leaders who "will stand up for the other side".<ref name="Georgetown Institute of Politics and Public Service"/>

====In the legal profession====
Penn State University conducted a study on perceptions of the legal profession and its relation to civility. They found that general opinion pointed to a drop in civility within the legal profession. To counteract demeaning and unprofessional behavior, there have been several initiatives put in place by state bar associations. However, the legal profession is not the only industry that has adopted civility standards. Many other companies and organizations across several industries have adopted civility standards that also help to increase workplace civility.<ref>{{Cite web |author=PennState University |title=University Libraries Civility Statement and Guidelines |publisher=Penn State University Libraries |date=2017 |url=https://libraries.psu.edu/about/diversity/university-libraries-civility-statement-and-guidelines |access-date=December 28, 2017}}</ref>

====In schools====
Numerous universities in the U.S., such as the [[University of Colorado]], the [[University of Missouri]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Civility, You, and Mizzou |publisher=University of Missouri |date=2015 |url=https://understand.missouri.edu/civility-you-mizzou/ |access-date=December 28, 2015 |archive-date=December 29, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171229052359/https://understand.missouri.edu/civility-you-mizzou/ |url-status=dead}}</ref> [[University of California Davis]],<ref>{{cite web|title=The Civility Project|url=http://civilityproject.ucdavis.edu/|website=civilityproject.ucdavis.edu|access-date=15 November 2016}}</ref> [[Johns Hopkins University]],<ref>{{cite web|title=JHU Dr. Forni's Civility Website|url=http://krieger.jhu.edu/civility|website=krieger.jhu.edu|access-date=15 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170203180522/http://krieger.jhu.edu/civility|archive-date=3 February 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[University of Wisconsin]],<ref>{{cite web|title=UW Oshkosh CivilityWorks|url=http://civilityworks.uwosh.edu/|url-status=dead|website=CivilityWorks|access-date=15 November 2016|archive-date=10 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110223721/http://civilityworks.uwosh.edu/}}</ref> [[Rutgers University]],<ref>{{cite web|last1=Lanman|first1=Sandra |title=Rutgers Project Advances Civility on Campus and Beyond|url=https://sas.rutgers.edu/news-events/student-news/1058-draft-2-rutgers-project-advances-civility-on-campus-and-beyond2nd-draft-for|website=Rutgers University, School of Arts and Sciences|access-date=15 November 2016}}</ref> [[American University]],<ref>{{cite web|title=What is Civility|url=https://www.american.edu/ocl/Civility.cfm|website=www.american.edu|access-date=December 28, 2017}}</ref> and [[California State University San Marcos]]<ref>{{Cite web |author=Student Life and Leadership |title=The Civility Campaign |publisher=California State University San Marcos |date=2015 |url=https://www.csusm.edu/civility/ |access-date=August 1, 2015}}</ref> have created programs designed to foster and define what civility means on their campuses. The Center on Civility & Democratic Engagement at [[University of California, Berkeley]]'s [[Goldman School of Public Policy]] recognizes that public dialogue often lacks civility and focuses on preparing leaders to successfully engage people of diverse perspectives in finding solutions for pressing public policy issues.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Goldman School of Public Policy Center on Civility & Democratic Engagement |url=https://gspp.berkeley.edu/centers/ccde |access-date=October 14, 2020}}</ref> Some colleges, such as the [[Arizona State University]], offer an undergraduate certificate in Civil Communication.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Certificate in Civil Communication |publisher=Arizona State University |date=2017 |url=https://humancommunication.clas.asu.edu/degrees/certificate-and-minor |access-date=December 28, 2017}}</ref> Other universities, such as [[Kansas State University]],<ref>{{Cite web |title= Institute for Civic Discourse and Democracy |publisher=Kansas State University |date=2017 |url=https://www.k-state.edu/icdd/ |access-date=December 28, 2017}}</ref> developed programs in dialogue and deliberation which involve codes of behavior that foster constructive, civil discourse. Although many colleges have adopted programs to foster civility efforts, there are still many colleges and universities, including many of the [[Ivy League]] schools, that do not have or list no visible place online about any civility initiatives, codes or standards.

====In the community====
Numerous community groups have formed in the U.S. to restore constructive civility in the public space. The Civility Toolkit with approximately 300 civility tools aggregated by the Civility Center provides access to resources regarding civility to help restore civility in society.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Civility Center |title= The Civility Center Toolkit & Resources |publisher=Civility Center 501(c)(3) |date=2015 |url=http://www.civilityresources.com/Civility-Resources.html |access-date=May 24, 2017}}</ref> Many of these groups are members of the National Coalition for Dialogue and Deliberation.<ref>{{Cite web |author=National Coalition for Dialogue & Deliberation |title=What We're All About |publisher=NATIONAL COALITION FOR DIALOGUE & DELIBERATION |date=2015 |url=http://icdd.k-state.edu/ |access-date=August 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160417082659/http://icdd.k-state.edu/ |archive-date=April 17, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

Arnett and Arneson define civility as "a metaphor that points to the importance of public respect in interpersonal interaction."<ref>{{cite book |last=Arnett, Arneson |first=Ronald, Pat |date=September 30, 1999 |title=Dialogic Civility in a Cynical Age: Community, Hope, and Interpersonal Relationships |url=https://archive.org/details/dialogiccivility00arne|url-access=registration |publisher=State University of New York Press |page=[https://archive.org/details/dialogiccivility00arne/page/7 7] |isbn=978-0791443262}}</ref> The difference between tolerating someone and respecting them is that toleration does not imply respect, but respect requires understanding of another person's perspective. Having [[social intelligence]] or "Social IQ" impacts our ability to empathize with people, and realize all people are human and that if respect or common ground cannot be met that we strive for at least toleration in order to be civil.

In ''Psychology Today'', Price-Mitchell describes civility as a personal attitude that acknowledges other humans' rights to live and coexist together in a manner that does not harm others.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}} The psychology of civility indicates awareness, ability to control one's passions, as well as have a deeper understanding of others. This may suggest that civility goes beyond mere toleration, but may imply a mutual co-existence and respect for [[humankind]].

In the academic journal ''[[Philosophy & Public Affairs]]'', Calhoun delineates civility as an element of dialogue that sheds light on "basic moral attitudes of respect, tolerance, and considerateness".<ref>{{cite journal| first=Cheshire |last=Calhoun |title=The Virtue of Civility |journal=Philosophy & Public Affairs |location=251–275}}</ref> Calhoun considers civility to be one of the moral [[virtues]] that can differ from what is socially acceptable, since what is socially acceptable is not always morally correct.

In the ''Washington Post'', Peter Wehner, author and former deputy director of speechwriting for President [[George W. Bush]], expressed three central points on how civility makes society function and noble. The first of these points illustrates that civility is what holds our families, communities, conversations, and establishments together.<ref name=Gerson>{{cite news| first=Michael |last=Gerson |title=Civility doesn't just make our system function – it also makes it noble |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/civility-doesnt-just-make-our-system-function--it-also-makes-it-noble/2019/06/06/f560c346-8881-11e9-a491-25df61c78dc4_story.html?noredirect=on |access-date=June 17, 2019}}</ref> Civility enables civic cohesion and eliminates excuses for invective conversations or conflict. Wehner's second point suggests that civility is also an expression of a work of divine art and respect for all human beings.<ref name=Gerson /> In some ways this mirrors the words written in the [[United States Declaration of Independence]] on [[Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness]] in that all people are worthy of the inherent and unalienable respect of human dignity. The third point made by Wehner is that civility is an expression of epistemological humility where truth is not relative, but suggests that truth can cover a more widely spread understanding than what is preconceived or imagined.<ref name=Gerson />

The [[Smithsonian Institution|Smithsonian]] coordinated with Olúfémi O. Táíwò, assistant professor of political philosophy and ethics at [[Georgetown University]], to discuss the important role that civility has played in the pursuit of [[social justice]].<ref name=Smithsonian>{{Cite web |author=Smithsonian |title= Civility's Role in Social Justice |publisher=2020 Smithsonian Associates and Smithsonian Institution |date=2020 |url=https://smithsonianassociates.org/ticketing/tickets/civilitys-role-in-social-justice |access-date=July 5, 2020}}</ref> The presentation outlined that civility seemed to have declined in recent years by increasing political and social polarization coupled with simplistic mass communication systems. Additionally, Táíwò examines [[social norm]]s, such as the formal female adult address of calling a woman "Ms.", as well as emerging norms of social etiquette that could encourage people to think and ask others about their pronouns.<ref name=Smithsonian/> Hosting community events around civility can lead to interesting conversations and can broaden perspectives, and as Táíwò points out, civility will continue to play an important role in how justice for all will be shaped in the future.<ref name=Smithsonian/>

====Masons and civility====
The Freemasons and members of the Masonic family have had a long history of fostering civil dialogue and building civil societies. Masonic Lodges represent a peaceful assembly of people that are of different places of origin, languages, backgrounds, and beliefs. The principles and tenets of Freemasonry aim to promote and restore civility in the United States and around the globe. In 2015, Grand Master Charvonia of the Grand Lodge of California declared May 25, 2015 to be the "Champion Civility Month", which encouraged Freemasons throughout California to make an effort to bring more civility into their local lodges and community.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Freemason.org |title= Champion Civility This May Freemasonry |publisher=Freemason.org |date= May 2015 |url=https://masoneriaweb.com/ |access-date=December 28, 2017}}</ref> Additionally, Freemasons from around the world have been working to repair civility through the Masonic Family Civility Project. This Civility Project was built to help raise awareness of civility, by providing social conversations, civility resources, multimedia education, and information for anyone to access.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Masonic Family Civility Project |title= Using Masonic Values to Promote Civility|publisher=masoniccivility.org |date= December 2017 |url=http://www.masoniccivility.org/document-resources/ |access-date=December 28, 2017}}</ref>

From April 30 to May 1 of 2019, an Urgency of Civility Conference was hosted in Washington D.C. at the [[George Washington Masonic National Memorial]]. Civility experts convened to discuss civility in arenas of government, education, media, community, and the workplace. During the conference, Congressman [[Emanuel Cleaver II]] made a presentation in recognition of Virginia Forni and her late husband, P.M. Forni, for their efforts on the Johns Hopkins Civility Initiative.<ref>{{Cite web |author=The Urgency of Civility |title= "Urgency of Civility" conference Held in Washington DC|publisher=civilityconvening.org |date= May 2019 |url=https://civilityconvening.org/front-page-features/conference-overview/ |access-date=June 17, 2019}}</ref> Advocates of civility shared their thoughts, ideas, and efforts to promote civility in various sectors. Attendees worked together to form action items required to help further civility initiatives, including innovative thinking, engaging the community, and maintaining steadfast persistence.<ref>{{Cite web |author=The Urgency of Civility |title= Civility was Rediscovered and Redefined|publisher=civilityconvening.org |date= May 2019 |url=https://civilityconvening.org/front-page-features/conference-overview/ |access-date=June 17, 2019}}</ref>

====In the workplace====
Studies and polls from 2014 indicate that Americans find [[workplace incivility]] to be a growing problem that has a negative impact on them and their duties at work. One study suggests 60% of employees think that their co-workers' irritating habits have negatively affected them at their job. In the same study, 40% reported that they are looking for another job opportunity because of a negative co-worker. These studies suggest that incivility in the workplace dampens productivity and has an adverse effect on an organization's bottom line.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Barbara Richman |title=Ten Tips for Creating Respect and Civility in Your Workplace |publisher=Lorman |date=May 28, 2014 |url=https://www.lorman.com/resources/ten-tips-for-creating-respect-and-civility-in-your-workplace-15463|access-date=August 17, 2015}}</ref> This data does not account for how many people encounter workplace incivility and are not sure what they can do about it. Furthermore, it does not take into consideration how many of these workplaces have civility tools or initiatives.

Various organizations, including the United States government, have taken steps to prevent incivility at work. One strategy is addressing [[sexual harassment]] cases, which the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) defines as unlawful in all states. This involves preventing [[gender]]-based mistreatment during employment or hiring. Harassment encompasses "sexual harassment" as well as [[workplace bullying]], cyberbullying, and threats.<ref name="eeoc">{{cite web | url = https://www.eeoc.gov/sexual-harassment | title = Sexual Harassment | publisher = U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission}}</ref> Although sexual harassment's illegality is widely accepted, it gained significant attention in the U.S. starting in 1964.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}} In the past, unclear legal boundaries resulted in more people experiencing unwanted behavior due to legal ambiguity. The term's clearer definition has enhanced workplace protection, but individuals need to actively contribute by speaking up and reporting incidents.

====Organizational behavior====
Human resource managers are aware of the effects of social behavior in the workplace. Inappropriate workplace behavior has led HR personnel to pay more attention to problems arising from incivility, bullying, and abusive supervision within organizations. Research concluded that incivility can have a negative impact of [[organizational behavior]], including: decreased satisfaction, reduced job performance, increased perceptions of [[injustice]], increased depression, and can lead to employees to experience psychological withdrawal.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Work and nonwork outcomes of workplace incivility: Does family support help? |journal = Journal of Occupational Health Psychology|volume = 16|issue = 1|pages = 95–111| author = S. Lim and A. Lee |pmid = 21280947|year = 2011|doi = 10.1037/a0021726 | url=http://scholarbank.nus.edu.sg/handle/10635/44631}}</ref>

Organizations are improving their workplaces by reducing incident rates and limiting liability. Some companies offer employees civility training specifically geared to foster civility by facilitating conversations about it. Research indicates that civility training shows a positive increase in respect, job satisfaction, and overall trust, while effects of incivility, cynicism, and employee absenteeism decreased.<ref>{{cite journal | title = The Impact of Civility Interventions on Employee Social Behavior, Distress, and Attitudes |journal = The Journal of Applied Psychology|volume = 96|issue = 6|pages = 1258–1274 |first1= M. P. |last1=Leiter |first2=H. K. S. |last2=Laschinger |first3=A. |last3=Day |first4=D. G. |last4=Oore | publisher = Journal of Applied Psychology, Advance Online Publication |pmid = 21744942|year = 2011|doi = 10.1037/a0024442}}</ref> The results suggest civility training can improve the workplace climate, foster a culture of positive behaviors, and minimize workplace issues.

===In Canada===
In July 2012, the President of the [[Federation of Law Societies of Canada]] addressed civility at the 5th Biennial International Legal Ethics Conference.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wooley |first=Alice |year=2013 |title= 'Uncivil by Too Much Civility'? Critiquing Five More Years of Civility Regulation in Canada|journal=Dalhousie Law Journal |volume=36 |issue=1 |page=239 |ssrn=2186930 |url=https://deliverypdf.ssrn.com/delivery.php?ID=396031102089029102030069095091100088058033095009026094104026117098087088111104064097029031099028051096054091125029023004127099111073000085023000119112102115085102088089039073069071085022001098008109070015067097030109127013097084004114098117081101094103 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231130182157/https://deliverypdf.ssrn.com/delivery.php?ID=396031102089029102030069095091100088058033095009026094104026117098087088111104064097029031099028051096054091125029023004127099111073000085023000119112102115085102088089039073069071085022001098008109070015067097030109127013097084004114098117081101094103 |archive-date= Nov 30, 2023}}</ref> In 2012, the Law Society of Upper Canada decided that Joe Groia was guilty of incivility to opposing counsel during his successful defense of John Felderhof on [[Insider trading]] and securities charges. On the same case, the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] confirmed the decision of [[Bar of Quebec]] that Giles Dore was guilty of professional misconduct because of an uncivil letter he wrote to a judge. This high-profile case brought a lot of attention to the legal definition of the word civility, and what it means to be civil in the legal profession. It has since defined a broader set of rules of what is legally considered civil in the court of law in Canada.

Since the Groia case, [[The Law Society of Upper Canada]] launched several initiatives to guard against incivility in the Canadian legal profession. To enforce its stance on civility in the Canadian legal system, they issued verbal warnings to lawyers who are not civil with judges and other lawyers. The counter argument against civility measures is that the new guidelines may inhibit their ability to defend their clients.<ref>{{cite web |title=Has the so-called civility movement already won? |work=National Magazine |url=http://www.nationalmagazine.ca/Articles/January-2015-Web/Out-of-order.aspx |access-date=2015-09-17 |date=2015-01-28 |first1= Justin |last1=Ling |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181127064722/http://www.nationalmagazine.ca/Articles/January-2015-Web/Out-of-order.aspx |archive-date=2018-11-27 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In January 2017, the B.C. & Yukon Freemasons in Canada stated civility was like The [[Golden Rule]]: "treating others as you would want them to treat you". This statement was in part to a recent civility initiative.<ref>{{cite book |date=January 20, 2017 |title=Freemason's Civility Initiative Outline|author=B.C. and Yukon Freemasons|publisher= Masonic Civility |quote= Civility can simply be defined as treating others as you would want them to treat you.|url=https://www.masoniccivility.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/freemasons_civility_initiative_outline.pdf}}</ref>

===In New Zealand===
At a recent address with Gisborne's top businesswomen in early 2016, Lara Meyer, an adviser to the Australian Government, cited incivility in the workplace has cost New Zealand approximately {{currency|15 million|code=nzd|passthrough=yes}} a year. Noting that Australia is also losing out about {{currency|26 million|code=nzd|passthrough=yes}} a year due to a lack of workplace civility.<ref>{{cite web |title= Counting the cost of rudeness |work=The Gisborne Herald |url=http://gisborneherald.co.nz/localnews/2255300-135/counting-the-cost-of-rudeness |url-status=dead|access-date=2016-05-24 |date= 2016-04-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160411123515/http://gisborneherald.co.nz/localnews/2255300-135/counting-the-cost-of-rudeness|archive-date=2016-04-11}}</ref> There could potentially be more loss that is unaccounted for in New Zealand businesses, as the cost of rudeness could be holding them back from working together more politely and agreeably.
